articles.title: Ministros do STF defendem Andrei a Lula e citam ameaça de Mendonça | G1
articles.standfirst: Pauta do encontro incluiu também criação de um ministério dedicado à segurança pública e a indicação de um nome para a vaga no STF que está aberta desde a saída de Luís Roberto Barroso.
articles.summary: Andrei Rodrigues recebeu defesa enfática de ministros do STF em reunião com Lula, mencionando que André Mendonça pretendia prender o diretor-geral da PF.
articles.body:
A ala de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) mais próxima de Lula (PT) fez uma defesa enfática do diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, durante jantar com o presidente, no último sábado (21).

Segundo relatos obtidos pelo blog , integrantes da Corte disseram que Andrei foi vítima em meio à crise institucional envolvendo a PF e que ele ficou isolado durante os desdobramentos do caso.

Na conversa, os ministros também disseram acreditar que André Mendonça queria até prender o diretor-geral da PF.

Em setembro, na condição de relator das investigações sobre o caso Master no STF, André Mendonça mandou afastar Andrei Rodrigues da direção da PF.

A decisão foi depois revertida por Flávio Dino, colega de Mendonça no STF.

Agora, a defesa de Andrei feita por parte dos ministros ocorre no contexto da criação do ministério da Segurança Pública, uma das promessas de campanha de Lula.

O ministério deve ficar com a gestão da PF, que sairia do guarda-chuva do ministério da Justiça, como é no desenho atual.

Integrantes do Supremo defendem que quem estiver à frente da nova pasta precisa ter condições de garantir autonomia e proteção às polícias.

A preocupação dos ministros é evitar interferências políticas nas investigações.

Na reunião, foi dito a Lula que, sem o trabalho de Andrei à frente da PF, muitos dos desdobramentos recentes poderiam não ter acontecido.

Entre as recentes atuações da PF, estão investigações como a Operação Carbono Oculto, o caso Master e as fraudes no INSS.

O jantar também tratou da escolha do próximo ministro do STF, que vai ocupar a vaga de Luís Roberto Barroso.

Lula reafirmou sua preferência pelo advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias. Já uma ala de ministros ligada a Alexandre de Moraes defende o nome de Rodrigo Pacheco, ex-presidente do Senado.

Na reunião também estavam os presidentes do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), e da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB).

Interlocutores de Lula avaliam, porém, que seria melhor encontrar uma terceira alternativa, capaz de produzir maior consenso. A possibilidade de uma mulher também foi mencionada nas conversas.

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Andrei Passos Rodrigues, diretor-geral da Polícia Federal. — Foto: REUTERS/Murad Sezer; Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: Moraes determina citação por edital após fuga | G1
articles.standfirst: Prazo para defesa prévia será de 15 dias. Ministro apontou que senador se 'evadiu' para os EUA, mesmo com passaportes bloqueados pela Justiça.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro terá 15 dias para apresentar defesa após Moraes determinar citação por edital, apontando que o senador se evadiu para os Estados Unidos.
articles.body:
O ministro Alexandre de Moraes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), determinou que o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) seja notificado por edital para apresentar defesa prévia na denúncia da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) pelo crime de calúnia contra Lula .

O documento foi publicado na tarde desta segunda-feira (23).

Na decisão, assinada na sexta-feira (20), o relator afirmou que o parlamentar "evadiu-se do território nacional" e encontra-se nos Estados Unidos , em "local incerto e não sabido".

Na decisão, o ministro destacou que o senador deixou o Brasil mesmo após uma determinação judicial de entrega de seus passaportes.

Moraes citou ainda que, já no exterior, Flávio divulgou documentos à imprensa e nas redes sociais e concedeu entrevistas tratando da própria saída do país, mencionando uma reportagem publicada pelo jornal norte-americano "The New York Times" em 5 de novembro.

"O denunciado Flávio Bolsonaro, não obstante o bloqueio prévio de seus passaportes por decisão judicial, evadiu-se do território nacional, encontrando-se nos Estados Unidos, em local incerto e não sabido", escreveu o relator.

Ao justificar a medida, Moraes citou casos anteriores analisados pela Primeira Turma do STF que tratavam da citação por edital quando o acusado tem paradeiro desconhecido no exterior e age com o objetivo de escapar da aplicação da lei penal.

Segundo o entendimento do colegiado, a fuga não pode servir como instrumento para paralisar o andamento de uma ação penal, nem justificar a suspensão do processo quando há demonstração de que o investigado tem pleno conhecimento das acusações.

"Efetivada a citação por edital, mostra-se regular o prosseguimento da Ação Penal, especialmente quando o réu, de forma deliberada, permanece em situação de foragido da justiça brasileira, não sendo admissível que a fuga constitua instrumento de paralisação da persecução penal e de frustração da aplicação da lei penal", declarou Moraes.

Flávio Bolsonaro e família chegam aos EUA — Foto: Reuters

A PGR denunciou Flávio Bolsonaro ao STF na última quarta-feira (18) por calúnia, com agravantes pelo fato de o crime ter sido cometido contra o presidente da República e divulgado em meio que facilita a propagação da ofensa.

“ Lula será delatado. É o fim do Foro de São Paulo: tráfico internacional de drogas e armas, lavagem de dinheiro, suporte a terroristas e ditaduras, eleições fraudadas.”

O inquérito foi aberto em abril a partir de representação da PF, que concluiu em seu relatório final, enviado ao STF em junho, ter havido falsa imputação de crime ao presidente da República.

Ao apresentar a denúncia, a PGR sustentou que a declaração ocorreu fora do ambiente do Congresso, em perfil pessoal na internet, e ultrapassou os limites da liberdade de expressão e da crítica política, não estando coberta pela imunidade parlamentar.

Após o encerramento do prazo de 15 dias para a resposta da defesa de Flávio Bolsonaro, a denúncia será submetida à Primeira Turma do STF, que decidirá se aceita a acusação e torna o senador réu no processo.

articles.title: Democrats unveil 2028 debate rules with new dark money restrictions — but there's a catch
articles.summary: The DNC's 2028 Democratic primary rules require candidates to denounce dark money from super PACs and 501(c)(4) groups to qualify for 12 debate stages.
articles.body: The 2028 election season is already off to the races. The Democratic Party released its rules of engagement for the next presidential primary season on Monday morning, outlining a framework for 12 debates and setting barriers for candidates hoping to compete. One key rule will have Democratic presidential hopefuls swear off dark money during the course of the primary election. "In the wake of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision, dark money and independent spending have exploded, increasing the influence of special interests in politics," a press release by the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said. "While the DNC does not have the legal authority to ban super PACs or dark money groups, we are requiring our candidates to denounce their involvement in the Democratic presidential primary, in line with Democratic Party values and our 2024 Platform, in order to qualify for the debate stage." HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS That includes money earned by both super PACs and 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations during the course of the entire primary. And the rule, according to a framework obtained by Fox News Digital, will rely largely on Democrats' own self-reporting. Each campaign must designate a go-between with the DNC whose job is to specifically identify and report spending by outside dark money groups. DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS If outside groups spend money on a specific candidate that said candidate did not approve, they must denounce the action to still qualify for primary debates. If the candidate does approve or request the spending, they are required to refund those dollars and provide proof of doing so. "This is a framework, and it's the first step. There's going to be more granularity that comes over the next few months as the field takes shape. So this is kind of the opening of a conversation," Democratic strategist John McCarthy told Fox News Digital on Monday. "I think it's good that we're having this opening of a conversation because it will put pressure on all of the candidates internally to sit and say, we're going to lock arms and embody our values as Democrats." Asked about whether the emphasis on self-reporting will be a strong enough guardrail given the lack of laws around dark money spending, McCarthy suggested pressure from the party base will help. "I think if someone doesn't wanna make that pledge, I don't think that they're going to be rewarded by our primary voters as someone who they want to move forward as our nominee," McCarthy said. And while the pledge explicitly talks about the primary, it leaves open the question of dark money spending in the general election. But McCarthy suggested that it would not hurt whoever the Democrats' eventual nominee will be. "I think that Democrat-on-Democrat fighting is not going to enhance us for the general election," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There needs to be a meaningful debate over ideas. But we need to be the party that's for getting money out of politics. I think any Democrat who you talk to wants to come to the general election as strong as possible and ready to fight with anything it takes. So, you know, I think that people are comfortable with doing whatever it takes to win the general election."

articles.title: New chip-export rules are a start. Congress must make them last.
articles.summary: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi called on Congress to enact permanent legislative safeguards for advanced AI chip exports following reports of suspected technology diversion and internal administration disputes during the Trump presidency.
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s new restrictions on Chinese access to advanced American AI chips through overseas data centers are a step in the right direction. But they follow months of warnings about suspected chip diversions and reported resistance from senior Commerce Department officials. Commerce acknowledged that the rules were written at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council.

Our national security cannot depend on who wins an internal administration dispute. Congress must put stronger, permanent safeguards into law.

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO amid revelations about his affair with a suspected Chinese Communist Party spy leaves serious questions unanswered: How did restricted American AI chips reach Chinese entities, and why did senior officials resist tougher restrictions?

These chips are essential to America’s economic and military strength. In the Chinese government’s hands, they can support weapons development, cyber operations and surveillance. We would never export aircraft carriers or nuclear submarines to our adversaries. We should be just as serious about protecting advanced chips.

First, establish who knew what and whether anyone interfered with enforcement. Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a potential Chinese spy. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But we need an independent investigation into what information she may have obtained, whether the relationship helped Chinese businesses access restricted technology and whether Jensen Huang played any role.

Commerce began investigating Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer formerly led by Alice Huang, in 2024 over suspected chip diversions to China. Investigators requested Nvidia records in May 2025 and inspected the company with Singaporean authorities that June, when Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list. After Nvidia’s general counsel reportedly contacted senior Commerce official Jeffrey Kessler , Commerce suspended its administrative inquiry when Justice requested the case for criminal investigation, according to Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.). But Commerce retains separate authority to restrict Megaspeed. Why hasn’t it placed the company on its Entity List?

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Treasury, State and the Pentagon pressed for restrictions. According to Axios , Trump authorized action against suspected chip diversion three times, only for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Kessler to resist implementing it. Commerce has not added a single company to its Entity List since October 2025 .

Rather than demand answers, Trump defended Lutnick , suggesting his delays may have prevented a “blowup with China.” Protecting America’s most sensitive technology cannot take a back seat to avoiding difficult conversations with Beijing.

Nvidia enjoyed extraordinary access to the administration. Huang recalled Lutnick telling him , “Whenever you need access to the president, the administration, you call us.” Trump was reportedly warned about the suspected intelligence relationship before Huang accompanied him to China in May, though he denies knowing about it. He defended Huang publicly, having previously backed sales of advanced H200 chips to China in exchange for a 25 percent payment to the U.S. government . Congress must determine whether Nvidia’s access influenced the restrictions officials imposed — or failed to impose.

Second, identify how restricted chips reached China and close those routes. Bloomberg identified restricted Nvidia hardware at a Shanghai data center connected to Alice Huang’s business network. WireScreen examined more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records , finding more than 540 specifying particular AI accelerators and a supplier network spanning 374 companies, including shell companies.

Keeping chips physically out of China isn’t enough. Chinese AI companies have sought to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at overseas data centers. The new rules will require licenses for certain advanced chip shipments to data centers supplying substantial computing power to companies in China and other restricted countries, with additional licensing requirements for shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil.

But regulations can be weakened or withdrawn. Commerce has already suspended a rule extending export restrictions to subsidiaries of blacklisted companies through January 2027 . Congress cannot leave these protections to the discretion of officials whose enforcement decisions are under scrutiny.

Third, Congress must put stronger safeguards into law. The bipartisan Chip Security Act would require measures such as location verification to identify diverted chips. The MATCH Act would tighten restrictions on semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The AI Overwatch Act would codify restrictions on advanced chip exports and strengthen congressional oversight of export licenses to countries of concern.

The Remote Access Security Act , which passed the House 369–22, would establish explicit authority to regulate foreign remote access to restricted American technology.

Congress should include these bipartisan measures in this year’s defense bill. The new rules are welcome, but they cannot erase the failures that made them necessary. America’s national security cannot depend on whether a Cabinet secretary fears confronting Beijing. Congress must pass these protections into law.

Raja Krishnamoorthi represents the 8th District of Illinois in Congress. He is a member of the Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the U.S. and the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee.

articles.title: Marco Rubio’s might-makes-right manifesto
articles.summary: In his speech, Rubio rejected the idea that “great nations” cannot “impose ourselves upon the world.”
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent speech to a group of Federalist Society lawyers was shameful but usefully revealing. It shows the mindset of a man positioning himself for a presidential run.

The Trump era has numbed us somewhat to official amorality, but it was still shocking to hear our top diplomat express such clear contempt for the rule of law, both globally and at home.

Rubio dismissed criticism of the Trump regime’s deadly attacks on boats in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean, which have killed about 250 people without due process or presentation of evidence of their alleged drug smuggling.

Speaking about the International Criminal Court, which is designed to bring accountability to the worst human rights abusers, and which the Trump administration is seeking to destroy , Rubio invoked a ruthless Roman general’s response to officials who tried to get him to comply with the law: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.”

Remember, this was in a speech to lawyers.

And it wasn’t just about defying globalists. Rubio demeaned American judges who have courageously held the line against the administration’s lawbreaking, as well as their “allies in the academy, the press, and the professional activist class.”

For “these people,” he claimed , the “fundamental purpose of the law — American and international alike — is to weaken the United States, to undermine its power to act, to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.”

That smear is as unconvincing as it is cynical. We’ve just witnessed an outpouring of patriotic activism and civic engagement. We’ve elected a historically diverse group of leaders who are energized to make the government work to better all of our lives.

Besides, have any of Trump’s political opponents weakened the U.S. as much as the Department of Government Efficiency’s attacks on our science and health infrastructure, the televised brutality of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, the president’s shredding of our alliances, his trade wars and “real” wars, and the utter dishonesty and corruption of this administration?

Not to mention MAGA’s repression of truth and honest history. Rubio’s speech was an example of the kind of whitewashed, faux patriotic history MAGA wants to impose on our schools. It was slathered in soaring r hetoric about the “irrepressible ambition” to “explore and conquer” that he says defines our “essential character.” He raved about the expansion of our “empire” and the great national accomplishments that were made possible because it is our heritage to act without “moral doubt.”

Rubio waved away criticism of slavery and the treatment of Native Americans and did not mention the violence of Jim Crow apartheid or many other aspects of U.S. history that might have benefited from some “ moral doubt ” on the part of our leaders.

Rubio serves a president who declares that the only constraint on his exercise of power is his own apparently nonexistent morality. In his speech , Rubio rejected the idea that “great nations” cannot “impose ourselves upon the world.” That worldview seems particularly dangerous in the nuclear age, and particularly sinister at a time when Trump openly displays his admiration for dictators like Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, who certainly act at home and abroad without displaying “moral doubt.”

Given that Rubio’s speech was essentially about wielding power, it’s not surprising that he praised the Federalist Society’s power-building strategy , a “long march through the institutions of American law” that funneled young conservatives into “pipelines to power” and enabled the society to “seize the levers of history — remaking the whole landscape of American politics and law, forever changing the course of the nation.”

Rubio may have forgotten that the Federalist Society likes to pretend it’s not a political project — despite pursuing goals such as repealing the New Deal — the same way longtime member Justice Samuel Alito pretends that the right-wing Supreme Court justices are not advancing a political agenda.

Or maybe Rubio figured there’s no reason for pretense given that the MAGA movement has openly declared war on anyone who opposes it, including universities, law schools, law firms and judges.

Rubio said those wins “were built on this insight: It’s not just about placing good judges in position to interpret the law; it’s about shaping the world in which they do so — the norms and values, the ideas and beliefs, the expectations and assumptions that underpin how they think and reason and act.”

“Who defines these things, and to what end — that is what power is.”

Trump administration officials have made it clear what they think of the norms and values, the ideas and beliefs, that have protected American democracy and the rule of law. They sneer at the very idea of checks and balances and are gearing up to impede the long-overdue oversight that the incoming Congress is preparing to exercise.

Rubio seems to think that Americans who just overwhelmingly rejected Trumpism will be ready in two years for a reprise of its abuses of power and resistance to accountability, its cruelty and its bullying robed in the language of American greatness.

I think he’s wrong. I have more faith in the American people and the new direction they have chosen.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.title: Trump says he spoke ‘directly and indirectly’ with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Jensen Huang
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board members about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, telling CNBC on Monday morning that he sought to provide assurances to address their concerns about national security.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board members about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, telling CNBC on Monday morning that he sought to provide assurances to address their concerns about national security. “I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.” The president’s acknowledgment of his role in the Nvidia board’s decision marks a highly unusual push by the leader of the free world to influence a decision of a major company. Huang’s reinstatement at the top of Nvidia sent stocks surging after the market slid last week. In the nearly hourlong interview, Trump cast himself as a central figure in Huang’s reinstatement, saying he spoke with the key players involved in the company. The president added that he spoke with Huang “after I made the deal, after the deal was finished.” “I called him up and I said, ‘I ask you to do one thing, Jensen, work hard,’” Trump said. “I didn’t talk about other things because he understands that. He understands it better than we do. He knows what to do and what not to do.” Earlier Monday, Nvidia said in a statement that it had received assurances about Huang from the U.S. government, though it did not name Trump. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the board said. Trump said on CNBC that the administration assured the company that Huang, who allegedly had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, did not pose a national security risk. “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.” Later in the interview, Trump took credit more directly for Huang’s reinstatement. Asked on CNBC whether he thought Huang would have been rehired without his intervention, Trump said, “I believe my intervention was very important.” When asked what he told the board to convince them to reinstate Huang, Trump said he changed the board’s minds. “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way, and I convinced them, and I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago,” the president said, pointing to the company’s stock price diving in the wake of the scandal and shake-up. In the interview, Trump also said “basically I was represented at the board.” Asked whether last week’s stock market losses affected his view on Huang’s return to Nvidia, Trump said, “probably so.” “But the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump said. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.” The president initially supported the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook being brought on to run Nvidia before he endorsed Huang’s return. Trump told CNBC that he did not think “anybody can do” what Huang does, referring to the company’s prospects moving forward. “I think Tim would have helped revive the stock, but I don’t think anybody could revive the stock like it’s being revived right now,” Trump said. Nvidia’s stock shot up and markets rebounded after the board’s announcement of Huang’s return. Trump also expressed concern that if Huang was not reinstated, China could try to recruit him to work for a Chinese company. “If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, “Hey, how would you like to come to China?” Trump said. Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Huang quickly drew blowback from the president’s critics on both sides of the aisle. Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said Nvidia should have “ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang.” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., accused the president of “selling out our national security to keep the stock market high.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, foreshadowed congressional investigations when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer, D-N.Y., said in the post. Asked on CNBC about Republican lawmakers who might be concerned with Huang’s return, Trump said, “When I speak to them, they’re going to be great.” Asked how he would respond to people who questioned why a president should get involve in the governance of a company like Nvidia, Trump said, “I’m doing it for the country.” Trump did not provide specific markers on how he would determine whether to get involved in an American company. “I can only say it’s touch, it’s feel,” Trump said. “It’s like a great golfer around the green. He’s got a touch, you know, the great ones. They have a way of just sort of hitting the ball just right. It goes up in the air and it lands and it rolls to the pin, and other people can’t do that. It’s touch.”

The meeting comes as some have called for a slowdown in AI development amid rising safety concerns. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

articles.title: Trump to criticize Newsom’s commutation of inmates facing execution at DOJ
articles.summary: Correction: A previous version of this article misstated the timing of California’s 2016 ballot initiative on the death penalty. President Trump will push back on California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D) move to commute the sentences of more than 548 inmates who were facing execution in remarks he is set to deliver at the Justice Department…
articles.body:
Correction: A previous version of this article misstated the timing of California’s 2016 ballot initiative on the death penalty.

President Trump will push back on California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D) move to commute the sentences of more than 548 inmates who were facing execution in remarks he is set to deliver at the Justice Department on Monday afternoon.

“Governor Newsom is failing these innocent victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these heinous murderers. He is playing politics with public safety. President Trump will always stand with innocent victims and will continue to restore law and order and deliver safer communities,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement.

Trump will be joined by Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and other members of federal law enforcement, including representatives from the Drug Enforcement Administration; U.S. Marshals Service; the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; and the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

Additionally, some family members of victims are slated to attend. Trump and administration officials will highlight victims’ stories.

The move could be seen as platforming Newsom, who is considering a 2028 presidential run.

Newsom announced earlier this month that he will commute the death sentences of all of the state’s inmates who were facing execution.

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values,” Newsom said in the announcement. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”

The governor noted that the inmates have inflicted “indescribable suffering” on victims, families and the state’s communities, noting that many Californians “feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die.”

“I do, however, pray that this action will finally separate the memories of the victims of these crimes from the fate of those who harmed them,” Newsom said. “We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims.”

In 2016, a ballot initiative that would have abolished the death penalty in California was defeated by just more than 6 points.

Newsom instituted a moratorium on the death penalty after taking office in 2019, effectively formalizing a de facto pause on the measure that had been in place in California since 2006.

articles.title: Emanuel suggests Schumer shouldn’t run for majority leader next cycle
articles.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel on Sunday suggested that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) should make it clear that he intends to serve only two years as majority leader. “If I was Chuck Schumer, what I would say is, ‘I’m going to secure the majority, I am not going to run for…
articles.body:
Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel on Sunday suggested that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) should make it clear that he intends to serve only two years as majority leader.

“If I was Chuck Schumer, what I would say is, ‘I’m going to secure the majority, I am not going to run for majority leader next cycle, and I’m going to make sure other — the young voices and faces of this party — grow. That would take the tension out of this,” Emanuel told ABC News ‘s Jonathan Karl on “This Week.”

Karl asked Emanuel if Schumer, who is facing a challenge from the left to lead the new Democratic majority, should serve as leader for the next two years.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Yeah, just get it over with. Chuck Schumer is a friend, as is Chris Van Hollen, but this is not what people voted for,” the former Chicago mayor replied, referring to the Maryland senator seeking to replace Schumer as Democratic leader.

“They voted to get their lives better, not yours,” Emanuel added.

Emanuel, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, has called for the age limit to serve in Congress to be 75. Schumer, who has led the Senate Democratic Caucus since 2017, turned 76 on Monday, while Van Hollen is 67 years old.

Emanuel also spoke highly of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is positioned to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history. He said Jeffries’s ascension “is a statement about America that we should take pride in” and told progressive critics calling for different leadership to give “me a break.”

“We’re a coalition,” Emanuel said. “You’re going to tell the most loyal coalition partner, the African American community, that the moment in history –– you’re not going to get it? The Black vote is the most significant, most loyal, most dedicated part of the coalition. … It tells me when you vote against him, you don’t understand the politics of the Democratic Party.”

Schumer and Jeffries have both faced opposition from some incumbent and incoming Democratic lawmakers who have called for new leadership after the massive blue wave in this month’s elections.

Van Hollen told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” that his support among Democratic senators is “north of 15, and momentum is in our direction.”

A Pressley spokesperson told Boston-based outlet WGBH that she “is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.”

articles.title: Alito will be Raskin’s biggest obstacle to Supreme Court reform
articles.summary: When it comes to reforms for the U.S. Supreme Court, we may soon see what happens when an irresistible force encounters an immovable object.
articles.body:
When it comes to reforms for the U.S. Supreme Court, we may soon see what happens when an irresistible force encounters an immovable object.

The force, propelled by public sentiment, is Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), a long-time advocate of judicial reform, who expects to chair the House Judiciary Committee when Democrats control Congress in January. The obstacle, anchored in obduracy, is Justice Samuel Alito, who sees himself as guardian of the court’s absolute authority over its own affairs.

Raskin has articulated an ambitious agenda for the Judiciary Committee, including ethics and procedural reforms for the Supreme Court. There is no shortage of good ideas . Many of them, in an ideal world, would draw bipartisan support.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The committee could begin with the court’s unprecedented use of its shadow docket , also called the interim docket, to issue major policy orders with minimal briefing and little or no explanation of the majority decision.

Under Raskin’s proposed SHADOW Act , the court’s use of the shadow docket would be restricted to cases of “specific, concrete, and irreparable injury,” with an explanation published within seven days.

Although recent shadow docket outcomes have overwhelmingly favored Republicans, often overturning carefully reasoned lower court decisions , the pattern might well be reversed in the future. Everyone would benefit from greater clarity and transparency from the court, in a reform with no actual political valence.

Under the proposed High Court Gift Ban Act , the justices and all other federal judges would be subject to the same $100 limitation per gift as members of Congress. This could be sensitive, given that it was obviously inspired by the extravagant gifts showered on Justice Clarence Thomas by billionaires.

The statute, however, includes an annual exception for “personal hospitality,” tied to the untaxed gift section of the Internal Revenue Code , set at $20,000 per person for 2027 .

The generous cap, which would apply equally to Democratic and Republican appointees, would be an improvement over the current rule , allowing nearly unlimited “ personal hospitality ,” subject only to disclosure. A leading conservative scholar, who otherwise celebrates the court, has suggested “that this lucre is unseemly” and “public servants should not be allowed to do these things.”

The Supreme Court Ethics and Investigations Act would establish the position of ethics counsel, tasked with advising “the justices of the Supreme Court, and their spouses, on matters of judicial ethics,” including financial disclosure, gift acceptance, political activity, conflicts of interest and recusal and the unauthorized disclosure of official court documents.

This statute should be acceptable to Republicans. The ethics counsel would be appointed by the chief justice, and consultations would be optional for the justices. Ethics opinions would only be advisory and would not be disclosed to the public. Limitations on firing the ethics counsel might be a sticking point, but that could be resolved during committee negotiations.

Other reform proposals for term limits or court expansion are far more contentious, and likely to be stalled by Senate filibusters or vetoed by President Trump. These three, however, should not be controversial, as they affect Democrats and Republicans alike.

Alito is against them all in principle. In a 2023 interview with the Wall Street Journal , he flatly declared that “No provision in the Constitution gives [Congress] the authority to regulate the Supreme Court — period.”

That might seem to directly contradict Article III , which establishes the court’s jurisdiction under “such regulations as the Congress shall make,” but Alito wasn’t bluffing. A short while later, he declined to recuse himself in a controversial case, issuing a statement that did not even cite, much less adhere to, the relevant federal disqualification statute.

Alito’s disdain for the authority of what he called “the other more powerful branches” is broad ranging. In a recent speech for the conservative American Enterprise Institute, he inveighed against legislative reforms, including but not limited to court expansion.

Nor does he acknowledge a public right to information about the court. In April 2023, a few months before announcing its adoption of a code of conduct , the Supreme Court unanimously issued a “ Statement of Ethics Principles and Practices ,” noting that “a Justice may provide a summary explanation of a recusal decision.”

Since that day, according to a Westlaw search, Alito has recused himself over 80 times without ever providing an explanation.

Alito’s hubris, which one scholar described as a belief that the court “isn’t, and ought not to be, accountable to any other government institution,” is important because he holds great sway with his colleagues, who evidently agree that their compliance with federal ethics laws is entirely voluntary. The court’s Republican appointees in turn hold great sway with Republicans in Congress.

By resisting even the most common-sense legislation, Republicans may ironically make it more likely that the next Democratic trifecta will pursue court expansion. Changing the court’s composition may be the only way to achieve meaningful reforms, but that is a discussion for another day.

In the meantime, Alito might paraphrase Paddy Bauler, Chicago’s legendary saloonkeeper and alderman: This court ain’t ready for reform.

Steven Lubet is the Williams Memorial Professor at the Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law. He is coauthor of Judicial Conduct and Ethics (5th edition).

articles.body:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) suggested Sunday that the current federal government is not effectively confronting the issues facing everyday Americans.

“This is a class that is diverse in, you know, lived experience, diverse in geography and, you know, that all of us, I think, are really aligned around this idea of affordability, and knowing that we are the folks who are most connected to what we just went through, as we’ve been talking to folks on the ground,” Flanagan told MeidasTouch’s Jack Cocchiarella, referencing the newly elected class of Democrats.

“What is so clear to me is that folks outside of the Beltway understand that s‑‑‑ is on fire, right?” she continued. “Things are on fire, and for whatever reason, that urgency hasn’t reached Washington, D.C.”

Flanagan won the race to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) in the midterms earlier this month, defeating Republican challenger Michele Tafoya. Her win came alongside sweeping victories for Democrats across the country that notched the party a majority in both chambers next term.

The victories came amid challenging political territory for the GOP in the lead-up to Election Day. The Republican Party was weighed down by issues like the unpopular Iran war, President Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns around the cost of living.

Democrats are set to go from 47 seats in the Senate caucus to 56 in January, Decision Desk HQ has projected .

Flanagan campaigned on issues like “Medicare for All,” universal childcare, increasing the minimum wage and expanding veterans’ healthcare. She has also criticized Trump’s Canada tariffs and pressed to “dismantle” Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with her state being notably affected by the Trump administration’s strict immigration agenda.

She also threw her support behind Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) in the Senate leadership race against incumbent Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.).

Earlier Sunday, Flanagan celebrated her historic win alongside Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska), saying the election of the first two Native American women to the Senate makes the Capitol “look a little bit more like America.”

articles.title: Oath Keepers founder ‘absolutely done’ with Trump
articles.summary: The founder of the Oath Keepers, a right-wing extremist group, said he is no longer a supporter of President Trump. In an interview with The Associated Press, Stewart Rhodes said he was “absolutely done with” the president. The Oath Keepers founder called the president “one of the very worst” traitors “in our nation’s history.” Rhodes…
articles.body:
The founder of the Oath Keepers , a right-wing extremist group, said he is no longer a supporter of President Trump.

In an interview with The Associated Press , Stewart Rhodes said he was “absolutely done with” the president. The Oath Keepers founder called the president “one of the very worst” traitors “in our nation’s history.”

Rhodes told the AP that his aversion to Trump began when other rioters charged in connection to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack received pardons from the president, while Rhodes’s sentence was only commuted. He also said the war with Iran went against vows from the president to stop foreign conflict, per the outlet.

“We elected him to end the corruption in Washington, D.C. ‘Drain the swamp.’ Unfortunately his administration has been one of the most corrupt administrations in U.S. history,” Rhodes said of Trump in the AP interview.

In August, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta “reluctantly” agreed to drop criminal charges against eight members of the Oath Keepers, including Rhodes , who were convicted for their participation in the Capitol attack. The judge granted a motion from the Justice Department to dismiss indictments against the members of the right-wing group.

Mehta said the government’s decision to step away from the prosecutions was “not in the public interest,” but there was no legal basis to deny it.

“This court does strongly disagree,” he wrote. “But that alone is not a valid basis to deny the motion. The court must give way to the primacy of the Executive Branch in making charging decisions.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after Trump says he 'made' the deal
articles.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
articles.body:
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back.

But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December.

His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal

In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

Congress vows investigations into Huang and Nvidia

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".

"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.

Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said.

"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate.

"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said.

Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a member of the House foreign affairs committee, also condemned the move in a statement to the BBC as "premature" before multiple investigations are concluded. Fellow Democratic Representative Andre Carson, a member of the House intelligence committee, told the BBC that "Congress needs a full accounting of whether any controlled technology was diverted" to China.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.

Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

articles.title: Trump’s unprecedented intervention for Jensen Huang crosses a dangerous line
articles.summary: Since when did the president of the United States become an unofficial member of the board of directors of a publicly traded corporation?
articles.body:
I have no idea whether Jensen Huang should be running Nvidia. Neither, I suspect, do most of the people who spent Monday morning either celebrating or bemoaning his unexpected return as CEO .

The allegations against him are dark. Affairs with employees, including a reported relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China , are not exactly minor concerns for the chief executive of a company whose technology is central to America’s national security.

On the other hand, Huang founded Nvidia more than three decades ago and turned it into one of the most valuable companies on earth . The idea that he might be uniquely qualified to lead it is hardly unreasonable. Plenty of brilliant entrepreneurs are deeply flawed human beings.

But I don’t particularly care whether Huang deserved to get his job back. That’s Nvidia’s problem.

What I do care about is a Semafor report published Monday morning that President Trump personally called into a meeting of Nvidia’s board to argue for Huang’s reinstatement. Hours later, the board announced that Huang was back.

I’m sorry, but since when did the president of the United States become an unofficial member of the board of directors of a publicly traded corporation?

At the time I’m writing this, roughly 80 minutes after the news broke, Nvidia’s stock is up around 30 percent on the day. That’s an almost incomprehensible increase in market value for a company of its size. Investors are clearly thrilled, and I understand why.

But imagine the share price had fallen 30 percent instead. Would the president’s involvement suddenly become more troubling? Would we be asking whether he had interfered in a decision that should have been left to the company’s directors?

I would hope we’d be asking those questions regardless of what happened on Wall Street.

A corporate board isn’t an elected legislature, and its members don’t have to be insulated from outside opinions. Directors consult lawyers, bankers, regulators, investors and other executives all the time. But they’re also expected to exercise their own judgment. That’s rather central to the whole concept of having a board.

Nvidia’s directors have fiduciary obligations that don’t extend to pleasing the president. They are not obliged to accept his preferred CEO, no matter how enthusiastically he makes the case.

I can understand the White House wanting to know whether the allegations surrounding Huang raised genuine national security concerns. Nvidia’s chips sit at the heart of an international struggle over artificial intelligence, advanced computing and military technology. If American intelligence officials concluded that Huang posed no security risk, the directors absolutely should have been told.

But according to Semafor, Trump didn’t simply authorize officials to communicate a national security assessment. He personally advocated for Huang’s return.

Those are two very different things from where I sit.

Consider a director who doesn’t want Huang back. Perhaps that director believes the allegations reveal serious weaknesses in his judgment. Perhaps there are questions about the company’s culture or the message reinstatement sends to employees.

Now imagine the president gets on the phone and makes it clear that he wants Huang running Nvidia. How much does that change the conversation?

We don’t know. The fact that Trump advocated for reinstatement doesn’t establish that he pressured anyone or caused directors to change their votes. They might have been moving toward the same decision already. But the question of influence doesn’t disappear simply because the outcome might have been identical without the call.

Presidents have always dealt with business leaders, sometimes aggressively. John F. Kennedy’s confrontation with the steel industry is one example. The federal government’s involvement in the automobile industry during the 2008 financial crisis is another, although the circumstances were obviously different.

I’m not suggesting there’s some absolute constitutional prohibition against a president speaking to corporate directors about their executives. There isn’t.

Suppose a future Democratic president personally contacts the board of a major technology company and urges directors to remove a CEO who’s publicly criticizing the administration. Or suppose a Republican president wants an executive reinstated because that person is politically loyal.

That’s a miserable way to think about the separation between political power and private enterprise.

Corporate boards should be free to make decisions without wondering whether disappointing the president will have consequences for their businesses.

Of course, Nvidia has every reason to maintain a productive relationship with Washington. And if Trump sincerely believes Huang is indispensable to American technological leadership, why shouldn’t he express that view? Presidents aren’t expected to be indifferent to companies that matter enormously to the national economy.

But there’s a difference between expressing a view and entering a boardroom debate over who should hold the top job. The president carries the authority of his office into every conversation, whether he intends to or not.

Nvidia’s board initially decided Huang should go . Now, suddenly, it reversed itself. Maybe new information changed everything. Maybe directors misjudged the commercial consequences of his departure. Maybe they simply acted too hastily.

All are possible, and all are matters the board should be prepared to explain to shareholders.

But adding the president’s personal involvement makes an already unusual reversal harder to examine on its own merits. Because if the president gets to weigh in on who runs Nvidia, it’s reasonable to wonder which other corporate leadership decisions might eventually become matters of presidential interest.

I don’t especially like where that leads. And I doubt many Americans would either.

Aron Solomon is chief strategy officer for AMPLIFY and has taught entrepreneurship at McGill University and the University of Pennsylvania.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers decry White House involvement in Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.summary: Congressional Republicans are crying foul over President Trump’s involvement in Nvidia’s decision to bring back Jensen Huang despite allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board of directors announced its decision to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive officer and member of…
articles.body:
Congressional Republicans are crying foul over President Trump’s involvement in Nvidia’s decision to bring back Jensen Huang despite allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced its decision to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive officer and member of the board Monday morning.

The company in a statement said it “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that Huang’s “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But some congressional Republicans did not share the same view, and are calling for investigations into all the national security implications of Huang’s leadership.

“No national security risk? Based on what?” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) wrote on the social platform X .

In another post , Cornyn elaborated on his questions about the situation.

“Again, did the FBI do a defensive briefing of Huang? If not, why not? If so, what did they tell him about the risk? Did he ignore it?” wrote Cornyn, who is leaving Congress next month after losing his reelection bid to Trump-backed Ken Paxton in the primary.

Republicans also want to look into the Trump administration’s ties to the company and the extent to which Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick enabled Nvidia to circumvent export controls over the objections of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) wrote on X . “Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?”

Trump said Monday that he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang, going so far as reportedly dialing into the company’s board meeting to argue for Jensen’s return.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump told CNBC of Huang being reinstated. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me a very important part of our country.”

Other Republican lawmakers similarly slammed the decision due to ongoing probes launched into whether Nvidia violated U.S. export controls against China.

Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) directly called out the tech firm for the decision, accusing Nvidia’s head of being “compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy.”

“Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang,” Bacon continued. “Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology.”

Huang founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago but resigned earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair.

Reports indicated he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Megaspeed who intelligence officials suspect had ties to China’s Ministry of State Security and was in contact with an official at the Chinese spy agency while she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang acknowledged in a public statement earlier this month that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and said he was “deeply sorry.” He resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia in mid-November.

“Ummm… she was, and is, a spy,” Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.) expressed on social media . “How about we get serious about making sure China doesn’t steal US company technology? Or get serious about not selling it directly and indirectly?”

The House Foreign Affairs Committee is slated to hold transcribed interviews for Jensen Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel to explain “potential breaches of national security.”

Huang is also slated to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), a member of the Banking Committee who just won re-election, wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement.”

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December,” Ricketts wrote.

Nvidia also confirmed it would still be investigating its CEO, who they say “fully supports” the probe and “is committed to cooperating with it.”

In the press release, the board of directors confirmed the vote was unanimous following multiple discussions and meetings with Jensen Huang, after which they were satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”

Throughout Jensen Huang’s departure and eventual return, President Trump has remained a strong ally of the tech CEO. He called on Nvidia multiple times to reinstate Jensen Huang and lauded this recent decision.

“The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , adding the U.S. “needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

articles.title: Zacharia says Miller took ‘significant pay cut’ to return to White House
articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Sunday slammed a recent report about White House chief of staff Stephen Miller’s salary, claiming he took a “significant pay cut” upon returning to work for President Trump. Forbes recently reported that Miller makes $195,200 a year but estimated that he has a net worth of $5…
articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Sunday slammed a recent report about White House chief of staff Stephen Miller’s salary, claiming he took a “significant pay cut” upon returning to work for President Trump.

Forbes recently reported that Miller makes $195,200 a year but estimated that he has a net worth of $5 million, mostly made from his time when Trump was not in office.

“Stephen Miller made money the way millions of Americans do — by working, building something, and investing as a private citizen,” Zacharia wrote on the social platform X . “How is that controversial?”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“He took a significant pay cut to return to government with a family of six,” she continued in the post. “He stayed loyal to President Trump and chose public service over higher private-sector income — the opposite of the classic revolving-door story.”

The ex-Trump aide also accused Forbes of being “garbage” and said casting “ordinary private-sector success as a moral failing says more about the outlet than about him.”

The outlet examined financial disclosures, nonprofit records and real estate documents it obtained. Adding to his finances was the $3 million sale of his Arlington, Va., home, after it was initially put on the market for $3.79 million in early October and later went down to $3.75 million.

His work after Trump’s first departure from the White House in 2021 included the launch of America First Legal. The registered 501(c)(3) organization garnered $6 million in its first year. He also saw gains from xAI stock, which Forbes attributed to his wife Katie Miller’s short-time work with Tesla CEO Elon Musk. The rest of the finances stem from bonds, cash and a federal pension.

Stephen Miller has long been an influential figure in Trump’s orbit. He previously served as a chief adviser to the president and has helped amplify the MAGA agenda, including on immigration.

He replaced former chief of staff Susie Wiles following the sweeping Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections earlier this month . Trump said Wiles had done an “outstanding job” and praised Miller as one of his “most trusted” advisers.

But Democratic lawmakers have bristled against the idea of Miller holding a key role in the Oval Office. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is set to become the first Black House Speaker, told The New York Times last week that he is open to working with Republicans to pass legislation.

As for the White House, Jeffries called Miller a “stone-cold racist” with “blood on his hands.” The New York Democrat had previously said that Miller’s “presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

articles.title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
articles.summary: Huang's role at the centre of his company's journey to lynchpin of AI proved crucial.
articles.body:
There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board .

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September , where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

articles.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's support for Trump.

They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media.

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

articles.title: Virginia, Oregon sue SpaceX over AI deepfake porn, child sexual abuse material
articles.summary: Virginia and Oregon’s attorneys general announced on Monday separate lawsuits against SpaceX for allegedly creating and promoting AI deepfake pornography and sexually explicit photos of children. Virginia’s lawsuit accused SpaceX of failing to prevent its AI chatbot, Grok, “from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent.” The lawsuits referenced marketing…
articles.body:
Virginia and Oregon’s attorneys general announced on Monday separate lawsuits against SpaceX for allegedly creating and promoting AI deepfake pornography and sexually explicit photos of children.

Virginia’s lawsuit accused SpaceX of failing to prevent its AI chatbot , Grok, “from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent.”

The lawsuits referenced marketing where xAI, which SpaceX acquired in February, advertised Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak” that would “answer spicy questions that are rejected by most other AI systems.”

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) said in a statement .

Jones called out Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode,” which is accused of allowing users to specifically create “nude and otherwise sexualized images.”

One study mentioned in the cases , by the Center for Countering Digital Harm, found the Grok account on the social platform X reportedly posted about 3 million sexualized images, including about 23,000 images that appeared to depict children, between Dec. 29 and Jan. 8.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield (D) said in a statement . “Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures.”

On Monday, X Safety wrote , “Sexual content involving minors, whether real or AI-generated, is abhorrent. It has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent.”

When “bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine,” the company said it acted quickly to “tighten its protections, the statement continued.

“We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors,” it concluded.

The dual lawsuits come after Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and media personality Paris Hilton held a press conference last week to push for the passage of the Defiance Act, a bill that would give victims a civil right of action to sue over deepfake pornography.

It already passed the Senate but is facing headwinds in the House during the lame-duck session.

SpaceX did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.body:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) will back President Trump’s pick to head the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Eric Ueland, ahead of his confirmation.

Punchbowl News reported on Monday that Curtis sought commitments from Ueland to uphold the GAO’s independence from the White House.

“The Senate has a responsibility to ensure that the person it confirms to this 15-year appointment can give Congress an impartial accounting of the executive branch, regardless of who is in the White House,” Curtis told Punchbowl in a statement. “With that, I understand the Committee’s decisions about how to proceed were outside Mr. Ueland’s control.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“Given his appointments in and affiliations with the current Administration, I needed clear commitments from Mr. Ueland that he would uphold that independence — which he provided,” Curtis continued. “If his nomination comes before the full Senate, I intend to vote yes and will exercise any oversight authority necessary to ensure he keeps his word.”

The Utah Republican met with Ueland last week after previously being concerned about Ueland’s ability to serve in the role as a “partisan pick,” according to Talking Points Memo .

Ueland told Democrats on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee last Thursday that he would not be “a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” and he said he plans to make the GAO “more effective” if confirmed, Federal News Network reported.

Ueland serves as the deputy director at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), where he has overseen controversial moves by OMB Director Russell Vought to cancel and rescind congressionally appropriated spending.

But the nominee faces skepticism from other GOP senators. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told The Hill last Friday that he’s insisting Ueland not be included in a larger “en bloc” package of nominations, which will all be voted on at once. He would prefer for Ueland’s nomination to be decided in a roll-call vote.

“He has a great reputation. He is a creature of this institution and other ones,” Tillis said. “Unfortunately, he’s going into a role that needs the utmost independence after coming out of an organization that’s one of the most hyperpartisan. … Doesn’t work. So for his sake, he shouldn’t be doing it.”

Tillis said he wants to avoid putting Ueland under “immense pressure” when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Republicans hold the majority in the Senate with 53 seats but will lose Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who will be replaced by Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), next month.

Ueland is “at the tail end of his career, and you know how this administration works,” Tillis said. “They could absolutely destroy him on the tail end. That makes him vulnerable to a lack of independence.”
