articles.body:
It’s Monday. Thanksgiving week is certainly NOT off to a slow start.

Programming note : Hello! We are Elliott Davis and Steff Danielle Thomas , filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to edavis@thehill.com and sthomas@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Markus Schreiber and Jeff Chiu

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12. Eleven days later, he is back at the helm.

The chipmaker’s board of directors announced Monday morning that Huang has been reinstated. The board also said its investigation into Huang — who stepped down after admitting to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang , who the U.S. intelligence community believes is a Chinese spy — will continue.

But the board also noted it received input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government before making its decision, saying it is confident Jensen Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. President Trump told CNBC later Monday that he “convinced” Nvidia’s board to put Jensen Huang back in charge.

While consistent Jensen Huang backers, including Trump and Elon Musk, said they support the reinstatement, the board’s move was met with swift backlash from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R), in a post on the social platform X, took issue specifically with Nvidia’s statement on getting input from the federal government: “No national security risk? Based on what?”

Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.), who is also leaving Congress, chimed in , writing that Alice Huang “was, and is, a spy.” Another outgoing Republican lawmaker, Rep. Don Bacon (Neb.), shared similar comments and said Nvidia “should have moved on.”

Meanwhile, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) — who is poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee come January — said in a statement that the Nvidia board made a “reckless decision” to bring back Jensen Huang. But she added that he and the company “still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls.”

Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before lawmakers for closed-door briefings next week. While he might be back in charge of one of the most valuable companies in the world, it’s unlikely that the pressure from Capitol Hill will calm down anytime soon.

The Trump administration and Republicans appear divided on the Pentagon’s $350 billion defense reconciliation package , as reports emerge that some GOP lawmakers are considering closing the tap on Iran war funding in the negotiation process.

The Hill’s Filip Timotija reports for Insiders that the massive defense package is looking increasingly doomed with mere weeks left in the lame-duck session. And Senate Republicans have previously warned that Trump’s push to rely on reconciliation — without requiring Democratic input — would risk a government shutdown with the Dec. 11 funding deadline looming.

CNN reported earlier Monday that top Senate Democrats and Republicans are discussing a deal that would cut off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran conflict in exchange for replenishing billions for the Defense Department.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), meanwhile, told The Washington Post he is “ open to anything that keeps the government funded and makes sure that we’ve got our military and national security requirements and needs met .”

There appears to be urgency from Republicans to reach a deal, with Democrats set to take the majority of both chambers on Jan. 3.

Trump is floating renewed strikes after the new year if the U.S. and Iran fail to reach a deal, accusing Iranian officials of dragging out peace talks.

Tehran, meanwhile, is threatening to confront the U.S. naval blockade following a fresh round of tit-for-tat attacks. The escalating tensions also come amid concerns over a possible “ dirty bomb ” plot, though the White House says there is no credible threat to the homeland.

Democrats are also clashing over how to wield their new Senate majority, with the chamber’s filibuster rules emerging as a major sticking point.

The divide? Progressives want to make it easier to advance their agenda, while moderates warn that changing the rules could come back to haunt them.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) is pushing a return to the talking filibuster, which would force opponents to hold the floor to block legislation.

📰 Read more here from The Hill’s Alexander Bolton .

There’s a high-stakes countdown underway in the Hawkeye State, where the U.S. Army has rescheduled its planned detonation of more than 60 barrels of highly unstable explosives.

The new date? Wednesday. The original detonation was postponed amid legal challenges from environmental groups warning of serious health and environmental risks.

The material, known as lead azide, could release toxic dust into surrounding communities, the critics warned. Some fear the contamination could linger for years.

There’s a catch : The Army says falling temperatures could make the explosives even more unstable, adding urgency to the operation.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) has activated the state’s emergency operations center to coordinate preparations with federal officials, while lawmakers are demanding more transparency about the risks and why safer disposal methods weren’t pursued.

articles.title: The Dow is now under 50,000. So how about releasing those Epstein files?
articles.summary: As the U.S. economy faces a downturn and a Democratic shift in Congress, President Donald Trump faces mounting pressure regarding his administration’s refusal to release millions of pages related to the Epstein files.
articles.body:
Did they think we forgot? Back in February, when brought before Congress, then Attorney General Pam Bondi infamously bought up the Dow Jones Industrial Average when defending her boss’s lack of transparency pertaining to the release of the Epstein Files.

“The Dow is over 50,000,” Bondi told Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.). “I don’t know why you’re laughing. You’re a great stock trader. As I hear, Raskin.” I guess the insinuation was that since the economy was perceived to be doing well, we could ignore that a major campaign promise of both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, as well as others in the MAGA-verse was being broken.

Of course, shortly after this, the U.S. decided to go to war with Iran. I am not going to sell you on a conspiracy that Trump went to war to distract from the Epstein files, but it didn’t look good for him, did it? That said, as we are drawing to a close of a very momentous and arduous 2026, we still have between 2.5 million to 3 million pages of the files still unreleased.

Bondi’s argument was bonkers then, but it also showed Trump’s mindset. As long as they could project that things were going well, even if they weren’t, then he would be absolved of his sins, real or alleged.

Of course, the Iran war didn’t go as planned. The Top Gun Maverick strategy of dropping a few bombs and calling it a day seems to work only in the movies. Instead, we have a protracted conflict that has caused a lot of economic pain in this country. Of course, that was a hoax until the midterm campaign. Then it became short-term pain that we had to endure while the oil and gas companies were raking it in .

You know who else was raking it in? Our president. Thanks to the Iran war, Trump’s holdings in oil and gas have netted him up to $86 million dollars, even better than last year’s $46 million . That is a lot of money to you and me, but it is chump change to how much Trump has made overall. He has grown billions of dollars richer while holding office during his second term. Some of that was due to a shady crypto deal . Some of it was the fact he was a businessman with a very diverse and voluminous stock portfolio who benefited from the stock market’s broad rise.

It seems that some people in Trump’s circle have also made money on the stock market or prediction markets based on what Trump said or did. Has the president himself benefited from this? Not that we can see, but when the people around you are making out like bandits, it makes you look complicit or incompetent or both.

We know there are two economies in the United States. The one for regular folks went off the rails a while ago. The one for rich folks was in its golden age. The message from Bondi and Trump was clear. You can’t get mad at us for not coming through if we are making you a ton of money. And boy did Wall Street, pushed by AI and tech stocks, make a lot of money for rich people.

The S&P 500 entered correction territory last week, even though it is bouncing back today. The Nasdaq had given up its 2026 gains before this morning, and the Dow is still below 50,000 as I write this. I wrote previously that the stock market was Trump’s Achilles heel . When it goes bad for the billionaires, it will surely go bad for Trump. Add to that an incoming Congress with a historic flip to the Democrats.

A good economy gives most presidents a lot of leeway with the people. But this was never going to work. We were always going to care about the Epstein files and getting justice for those who broke the law. It was just a matter of time. Corruption was a leading issue for voters in this past midterm election. That corruption goes back to prediction markets, self-enrichment, and deals for family members. That focus on corruption will also lead to the biggest headache for Trump heading into 2027.

Those files should have been released long ago. Why Trump has fought so hard to prevent their release is not known yet, and it would be wrong to assume anything. But it also didn’t make him look trustworthy. But I guess we had to wait for the economy to falter before we could hold him to task for covering up for his friend Jeffrey Epstein.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the 2025 Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: Schumer: Democrats will use ‘full power’ to probe Huang, Trump, Nvidia executives
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said Monday that Democrats will use their “full power” to investigate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other executives at the company after Huang was reinstated. “The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act,” Schumer said Monday morning in a post on the…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said Monday that Democrats will use their “full power” to investigate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other executives at the company after Huang was reinstated .

“The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act,” Schumer said Monday morning in a post on the social platform X . “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat.”

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” he added.

The post from Schumer, who is likely the next Senate majority leader in the upcoming Congress, follows Huang being reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO. Huang returned to the role a little more than a week after he stepped down amid an affair scandal reportedly involving an alleged Chinese spy.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said in a statement Monday.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” he continued.

Trump, who is an ally of Huang, lauded Nvidia’s board of directors over Huang’s reinstatement, saying it “made the correct and proper decision.”

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump said on Truth Social.

The president later said he convinced Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back.

The Hill has reached out to the White House and Nvidia for comment.

articles.title: Trump admin announces sweeping measure to cut Iran’s ‘last financial lifeline’
articles.summary: The Treasury Department blacklisted Iranian exchange houses and front firms in Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey accused of moving billions for Iran.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Treasury Department on Monday imposed sweeping new sanctions against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, overseas front companies and financial operatives accused of moving billions of dollars through a global "shadow banking" network to keep Iran connected to international trade. The action, carried out by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), targeted "financial plumbing" spanning Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey that officials say enables Tehran to bypass U. S. restrictions, sell oil and petrochemicals, and settle transactions in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan. "Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote in a statement Monday before the news release. "Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake." TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN ‘SUFFOCATING’ REGIME AS OIL WELLS COULD SHUT WITHIN DAYS, BESSENT SAYS Monday’s designations mark the latest escalation under Operation Economic Outcast, a maximum financial pressure campaign Bessent launched on Aug. 24, to cut off the regime's remaining revenue streams and heighten secondary sanctions risks for foreign banks and brokers that continue doing business with Tehran. TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE According to the Treasury Department, Iran's "shadow banking" apparatus is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on domestic currency exchange houses paired with bank-affiliated "rahbar companies" that manage sanctions-evasion networks through thousands of foreign shell firms. As declining oil revenues and existing sanctions squeeze the Iranian economy, Treasury said shadow banking facilitators have increasingly failed to repatriate export earnings while enriching themselves with state funds. The Treasury also revealed Monday that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) "identified approximately $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking." MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’ Among the highest-profile targets in Monday’s package is the Iran-based Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which matches Iranian exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to buy goods abroad across tens of billions of dollars in annual trade. Treasury noted that the Central Bank of Iran also uses bonds issued by the exchange center to facilitate cross-border trade in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan without relying on the U.S. dollar. BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY The OFAC package sanctions Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company — the rahbar affiliate for Iran’s Bank Sarmayeh — along with three of its senior officials, Sayyed Mohammad Jalali, Valiollah Hemmati and Ali Kalhor, for facilitating transactions on behalf of major Iranian oil companies. Two Iran-based currency dealers, Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company and Mellat Exchange Company, were blacklisted alongside five of their owners and officials. US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS To choke off Tehran's overseas payment channels, Treasury targeted 10 exchange house front companies across the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong accused of moving billions of dollars for Iranian clients. Those include Dubai-based Recaz Star General Trading LLC, which sent and received hundreds of payments totaling more than $170 million tied to Sadaf Exchange, and OGA Global General Trading L. L. C, which oversaw millions of dollars in payments for the state-owned National Iranian Tanker Company. Other newly sanctioned front companies include Hong Kong-based Grandez Trading Limited, Turkey-based Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi and several Dubai-based trading firms — including Gespl International General Trading LLC, which Treasury alleged was used by the National Iranian Oil Company to launder oil and petrochemical proceeds, and Robust Trading LLC for processing payments for the sanctioned National Iranian Copper Industries Company. articles.title: Vance personally pushed for Huang’s reinstatement
articles.summary: Vice President Vance was personally involved in President Trump’s push to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill on Monday. The source cited Vance’s long-standing relationships in Silicon Valley and standing in the tech industry as putting him in a good position to influence Nvidia’s…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance was personally involved in President Trump’s push to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill on Monday.

The source cited Vance’s long-standing relationships in Silicon Valley and standing in the tech industry as putting him in a good position to influence Nvidia’s board.

Additionally, the source credited Huang with being the top figure in protecting open-source models and putting a check on closed-source companies like Anthropic and OpenAI from becoming too powerful.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The source noted Trump and Vance were briefed on the national security elements of the matter, adding that the two did not see any evidence that Huang engaged in any activity that was illegal or harmful to U.S. national security.

The details of Vance’s involvement in the White House push to reinstate Huang come hours after the company announced Huang was back in the company’s top leadership role after he was removed for several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump detailed his role in leading the charge to reinstate Huang during a lengthy CNBC interview on Monday.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” the president told the network. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me a very important part of our country.”

Vance on Monday shared a video clip on the social platform X of Trump telling CNBC about Vance’s role in lobbying for Huang’s return.

In a separate Truth Social post, Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche said the government has no evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

However, Democrats and some Republicans on Capitol Hill are not as convinced.

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a post on X.

Meanwhile, Sen. Pete Ricketts (Neb.) was among multiple Republicans who said they still had questions.

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December,” Ricketts said.

articles.title: Bill Maher stunned as liberal guest blames DOGE for Palisades fire
articles.summary: This isn’t a mystery we need to solve: We know who started the fire, and now we are going to punish him accordingly.
articles.body:
We have a conviction in the case of the 2025 Palisades fire that devastated the Los Angeles area. Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was found guilty of arson — he deliberately started the blaze that destroyed thousands of homes and killed 12 people.

Prosecutors had argued that his motivation was pathological hatred of wealthy people who he believed were ruining society. His internet search history betrayed support for Luigi Mangione, the left-wing terrorist who killed a healthcare CEO and has attracted an odious level of sympathy. Rinderknecht worked as an Uber driver, and ranted to passengers about his anger right before he decided to take it out on the innocent citizens of LA.

In saner times, this conviction might prompt us to think about how demonization of the wealthy is often a form of mental illness that drives a person to do terrible things, and perhaps the left-wing drive to do just that — blame all of society’s problems on people like Elon Musk — is a bad tendency. But no, progressives are maintaining that actually Elon Musk is the real culprit here, because of DOGE.

Seriously, that’s what MSN Now’s Jacob Soboroff had to say about it. Watch this , from this weekend’s episode of “Real Time with Bill Maher.”

Talk about blame shifting! The fire was the result of one man’s actions. No, it wasn’t Elon Musk: it was the arsonist, a deranged person who hated the wealthy. It wasn’t DOGE, and it wasn’t climate change — those are convenient scapegoats, but it isn’t true.

First, the idea that climate change is responsible for widespread environmental catastrophe is very popular on the left, but it’s a false notion. You probably keep hearing that extreme weather events are becoming more frequent in modern times due to climate change, but of course, progressives always fail to note that actually fewer people die due to extreme weather than at any other point in human history. Earthquakes, hurricanes, tornadoes, heat waves and floods are all less deadly than they were before.

The claim that DOGE is at fault for the Palisades fire is, if anything, even more of a conspiracy theory. Liberals want to give you the impression, I suppose, that Elon Musk came in to power and fired all the firefighters, or something. Of course, he did no such thing. This July, U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz testified that our wildfire readiness response capacity was as strong as ever.

Again, this isn’t a mystery we need to solve: We know who started the fire, and now we are going to punish him accordingly. He was a resentful loner who admired a left-wing terrorist: the kind of person who hates Elon and the wealthy and the successful. Talk about an inconvenient truth.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle vowed to press ahead with investigations into the once-again Nvidia CEO, who’s scheduled to meet with them next week.
articles.body: The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill. “You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy. In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.” “No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X. President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.” “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.” Lawmakers made clear they still need answers. The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement. A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1. “There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement. In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.” “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida. The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.” But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.” “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” “Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said. Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips. Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny. “Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media. “Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.” “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.” Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”

articles.title: Trump considered firing Lutnick until he donated to presidential library
articles.summary: A Cabinet secretary reportedly on the verge of losing his job suddenly appears to have a new lease on life after making a massive contribution to the president’s library.
articles.body:
There may be no better example of how folks can buy access and good grace from the president than the latest controversy surrounding Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

According to a new report in The Wall Street Journal , President Trump was reportedly close to firing Lutnick, particularly after the secretary acknowledged visiting Jeffrey Epstein’s private island with his family. But then something apparently changed.

That something may have been to the tune of $25 million.

The report in the Journal said “Lutnick, a billionaire and former chairman of Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald, made a $25 million donation to Trump’s presidential library, and Trump stopped talking about replacing Lutnick.” Voila!

A Cabinet secretary reportedly on the verge of losing his job suddenly appears to have a new lease on life after making a massive contribution to the president’s library.

And we now know Lutnick’s problems extend well beyond his Epstein connections.

He’s also currently facing criticism over the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become part of the broader controversy surrounding Nvidia and U.S. restrictions on advanced AI chips. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly pointed fingers at Lutnick’s Commerce Department, questioning why the company wasn’t placed on a national security blacklist.

That disagreement has now spilled into public view, with Republican Sens. Thom Tillis, Tom Cotton and John Kennedy among those raising concerns.

Kennedy made his position crystal clear Sunday on “Meet the Press.” When Kristen Welker asked whether U.S. national security had been put at risk because of the Jensen Huang crisis, he had this to say :

“It appears to me — I emphasize appears — that the Department of Commerce has allowed the Communist Party of China to circumvent our export controls on advanced chips. Either that or they didn’t know what they’re doing, they’re so incompetent you wouldn’t put ’em in charge of a food truck.”

Kennedy went even further, suggesting the administration needs to get both Lutnick and Bessent under oath to explain what happened:

“It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying ‘stop it.’ So I want to get both of ’em in front of a committee, put ’em under oath, ask ’em not to stab each other, because I realize they don’t like each other. And let’s answer some hard questions.”

We’re talking about the Commerce Department, an agency responsible for protecting American economic and technological interests at a time when competition with China is one of the country’s biggest national security challenges.

If a Cabinet secretary can survive controversy after controversy, criticism from fellow Republicans and questions about national security, while reportedly benefiting from a multimillion-dollar donation to the president’s library, we shouldn’t expect accountability from this administration or the Republican senators who have been blindly loyal to it.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Warren, Hawley question CVS Health on proposed breakup
articles.summary: Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) on Monday inquired about CVS Health’s intention to break up into two separate companies, saying the move will not do enough to address the healthcare giant’s “anticompetitive” behaviors. In a letter to David Joyner, the CEO of CVS Health, the senators wrote the proposed separation would “continue…
articles.body:
Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) on Monday inquired about CVS Health’s intention to break up into two separate companies, saying the move will not do enough to address the healthcare giant’s “anticompetitive” behaviors.

In a letter to David Joyner, the CEO of CVS Health, the senators wrote the proposed separation would “continue to enable the company to drive up prices and crush competition.”

A spokesperson for CVS Health confirmed Joyner received the letter and will respond directly.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

CVS Health announced plans on Nov. 4 to separate into two companies — one focused on healthcare and another focused on pharmacies — in the first half of 2028.

The slimmed-down CVS Health, led by Joyner, will include insurance company Aetna, pharmacy benefit manager CVS Caremark and Oak Street Health, which provides primary care to older adults.

The roughly 9,000 CVS pharmacies, meanwhile, will fall under the new CVS Pharmacy umbrella. Prem Shah, the group president of CVS Health, will lead the new entity.

While Warren and Hawley wrote the breakup of CVS is “good news,” they still raised concerns about the resulting structure of the two companies and how that would impact healthcare costs.

Aetna and Caremark, the senators argued, would still be incentivized to “steer patients and prescriptions to the specialty pharmacy and affiliated medical providers” and “reimburse those affiliated at higher rates than independent competitors.”

The senators also asked Joyner to provide the last five years of financial information for CVS’s subsidiary companies by Dec. 9.

Warren and Hawley, while on opposite sides of the aisle, have taken populist approaches to rising healthcare prices. The two teamed up in 2024 to introduce legislation that proposes banning pharmacy benefit managers (PBM) from owning pharmacies.

The Massachusetts Democrat is in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee come January, while the Missouri Republican is on the Senate Health , Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

In their letter to Joyner, Warren and Hawley also cited legislation they introduced in February to crack down on healthcare conglomerates that control multiple facets of the industry.

Their Break Up Big Medicine Act proposes prohibiting parent companies from owning a medical provider or management services organization and a PBM or insurer.

Joyner said on CNBC earlier this month the legislation was one of the “external” factors CVS Health took into account before deciding to split into two companies.

But CVS Health’s new structure would “still be unlawful” under the bill, Warren and Hawley wrote Monday, adding the “vertically integrated” arrangement will allow the company to evade laws “intended to rein in corporate profiteering” at the expense of patients and taxpayers.

They also said CVS may be breaking up to avoid investigations the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could take pursuant to the legislation, which Warren and Hawley noted they intend to pass.

“Whether your intent is to try to head off regulatory pressure, or to cast free less profitable parts of the business, we are concerned that the new entity will still be a vertically integrated health care conglomerate with costly implications for patients and providers,” they wrote.

articles.title: Trump accused of 'socialism, communism' after helping scandal-plagued Nvidia CEO reclaim top job
articles.summary: Sen. Ruben Gallego calls Trump's role in Jensen Huang's Nvidia return "as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen."
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Republicans blasted Democrats on the campaign trail for pushing a socialist and communist agenda, but President Donald Trump’s involvement in getting Jensen Huang’s old job back has some lawmakers claiming hypocrisy. "This is as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital. "I mean, it's essentially state planning of private economies, and it's a whole new level of hypocrisy," he continued. "But the Republican Party definition of socialism is any government program, or government power, as long as the president doesn't like it or use it." Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang Tuesday morning after allegations that the tech executive had a handful of affairs, notably with an alleged Chinese spy, placing him back at the top of the chip juggernaut after two weeks out of the gig. TRUMP ‘DIRECTLY AND INDIRECTLY’ INTERVENED TO GET NVIDIA’S CEO REINSTATED, POTUS SAYS The company’s chips power myriad technologies that the Trump administration has pinned as critical to national security, including data centers and artificial intelligence, which lawmakers fear would be disastrous to fall into the hands of the Chinese government. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who has been hawkish on China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, told Fox News Digital that the company’s board was "free to vote however they want, but the federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened." "This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang’s actions on our national security and economy," Scott said. "Congress needs to be fully briefed on this as soon as possible, so we can take appropriate action if need be." TRUMP OFFICIALS TOLD 'NOT TO STAB EACH OTHER' AMID DEMANDS NVIDIA DISPUTE BE PUT UNDER OATH IN CONGRESS The company’s stock spiraled and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle raised national security concerns about China’s access to Nvidia’s chips. They have since pushed for stricter export control legislation and demanded that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify on the Hill. Trump, in an appearance on CNBC shortly after the board’s announcement, said he didn’t believe Huang would have been reinstated without him as he lauded the stock market’s upward trend. "The answer is no," Trump said. "I believe my intervention was very important." The Trump administration has not been shy about turning the government into a pipeline to the corporate world. The Cato Institute found in a report released in October that the administration has equity stakes in about 40 companies — though Nvidia is notably not on the list. TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT And Trump’s intervention did not stop Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., from plowing ahead with a scheduled hearing with Huang. He announced that the embattled, newly reinstated CEO would appear before the panel on Dec. 3. Gallego, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News Digital in a brief interview that "it really frightens me about what's happened with our national security," and questioned whether Trump had engaged "in stock market manipulation before making these announcements." "All these things, you know, are really now up in the air," he said. "And at the core, the question is, what's going to happen to our national security?" And Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has made AI safeguards a center of his challenge against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital that Huang was "at the center of this political corruption and political rot, and he seems to have been given a free hand by President Trump when it comes to formulating the Trump administration's AI and chips policy." The lawmaker is also a member of the Banking Committee, and said he was keenly interested in Huang's "efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he's been accomplishing that, how he's been getting his way with the administration." "And then obviously, the concern is that it is undermining our national security interests. After all, high-end chips can be used by the military in China," Van Hollen said. "And it's completely it's just completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take off all the brakes on AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead, if we don't, when in fact, it's the Trump administration that's helping China leap ahead." Senate Republicans are equally uneasy about the national security implications of the move, despite Trump assuring in a post on Truth Social that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security." "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said on X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, also told Fox News Digital that it was Nvidia’s right to reinstate Huang, but that the CEO needed to answer for what happened. "Jensen Huang’s actions raised national security concerns, and he must answer for them," Britt said. "The Commerce Department also has a responsibility to explain the role it played in allowing for potentially serious threats to our national security." "I look forward to having both Jensen Huang and Secretary Lutnick in front of the United States Senate Banking Committee, where my colleagues and I can ask questions and conduct necessary oversight," she continued. The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return sends China a clear message: The AI race is on
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return signals a renewed fight to win the AI race with China, as H200 sales end and Blackwell and Rubin chips lead the world.
articles.body: F. Scott Fitzgerald, author of "The Great Gatsby," once wrote: there are no second acts in American lives. Newly restored Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is about to prove that wrong. Let’s hope Huang returns to Nvidia chastened and ready to roll up his sleeves and get back to work helping America win the AI race with China. Jensen Huang is perhaps the most consequential CEO of our time. Huang’s return is a loud and clear message to China. The fight is on for the U.S. AI tech stack to prevail, not only in quality, but by winning dominant global market share. Huang famously wanted to fight to keep selling mid-level Nvidia chips in China as well as globally. That is why, in part, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security opened up review of export licenses "for Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X, and similar chips on a case-by-case basis provided certain security requirements are met." That’s over; even with the policy change, Chinese companies like Tencent and Alibaba have bought relatively few H200 chips, and Nvidia recently stopped H200 sales to China. TRUMP ‘DIRECTLY AND INDIRECTLY’ INTERVENED TO GET NVIDIA’S CEO REINSTATED, POTUS SAYS But it’s what comes next that makes Huang’s return important. Nvidia’s product line is at the center of the AI race. Nvidia was not selling China its best chips. The H200 is from the "old" Hopper line launched in 2022 and widely available. Nvidia’s "new" chip is the Blackwell series, which contained a new architecture and debuted in 2024, while the next step up is the Rubin series. The top Blackwell processes at 15 petaFLOPS, while Rubin hits 50 petaFLOPS in a "sparse" measure. It’s an oversimplification, but you get the point. The Nvidia chips are world leaders. You know China’s playbook. Undercut on prices, erode competitors, capture market share and then achieve lockout. It’s happened with solar panels, shipbuilding, and, of course, permanent rare earth magnets, where China controls 95% of the market share. The U.S. and allies are clawing their way back in rare earths. We can’t let the same situation develop in AI. TRUMP DEFENDS JENSEN HUANG'S CREDIBILITY, NVIDIA'S FUTURE AFTER BOARD REINSTATED CEO, SAYS 'SEX SELLS' The U.S. AI tech stack has to win global market share and prevent China from doing so. Talk to any of the Magnificent 7, and the strategy is basically the same for all the top tech companies. Their global business denies sales to China and generates cash for more investment in the AI ecosystem. What is different about AI is that this wider global adoption of U.S. tech is actually crucial to spurring continued innovation. That means taking precautions, but going ahead with business abroad. Like it or not, tech titans like Huang and Elon Musk, whose SpaceX provides 95% of U.S. space launches, are frontline national security players. Their ability to conquer market share is the new bedrock of U.S. economic security. Want an example? Take overseas data centers. "Those have to be located locally," Microsoft President Brad Smith explained on CBS’ "Face the Nation" on Sunday. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD Turns out cloud services must be near their users for peak efficiency and innovation, which is why Amazon Web Services alone says it has installed over 20 million kilometers of fiber-optic cabling to get "faster data transfer, reduced latency, and enhanced application performance." Speedier data spurs innovation. For the same reasons, Meta’s self-described global fleet includes data centers in Singapore, Denmark, Ireland, and Canada. AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR In this light, President Donald J. Trump’s comments on Friday about taxing AI data centers built abroad struck a discordant note—like he had the briefing slide upside down. Yes, we want facilities like Google’s data center at Waltham Cross, in Great Britain, which opened in late 2025, just after President Trump’s state visit. Their ability to conquer market share is the new bedrock of U.S. economic security. And with Huang’s return, an all-star player for Team USA is back. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM REBECCA GRANT

articles.title: Dems brush off Elon Musk's anti-MAGA pivot, warn DOGE probe still coming
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers call Elon Musk an "opportunist" and a "chameleon" after his MAGA remarks, warning of possible DOGE oversight probes in January.
articles.body: Democratic lawmakers are labeling Elon Musk an "opportunist" after the billionaire denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections. "I think that Mr. Musk is an opportunist," Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I think he's a chameleon. I think he will be whatever benefits him and his business." "It sounds like buyer's remorse to me," Rep. Christian Menefee, D-Texas, said. "Maybe he should spend his time focusing on his businesses instead of trying to buy politicians." I SAW THE REAL DOGE FROM THE INSIDE. WHY THE MEDIA GOT DOGE AND ELON ALL WRONG The political flip-flop callout comes after Musk made comments distancing himself from President Donald Trump and Republicans on Wednesday during The New York Times' DealBook Summit. Musk has put millions of dollars toward Trump, has previously campaigned with him and worked for the administration. "Whatever," Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said when asked about Musk’s comments. "That’s my response. Whatever." Musk has also been facing wrath from Democratic lawmakers as a potential target of oversight investigations for his time as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). "You're the architect of DOGE," Carter continued. "You wreck people's lives. You tear people's opportunities and their careers apart in a reckless effort to so-called save money when nobody's pocket's been padded with his. If he really wants to do the right thing, demonstrate it, not in word, but in deed." "I’m certain that he will be the subject of investigations," Rep. Sanford Bishop Jr., D-Ga., said. "We’ll deal with it when we deal with it." An investigation into Musk and DOGE seems to be at the top of the list for many Democrats as the party pushes for investigations to look into alleged corruption under the Trump administration after the party took back majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. "I've not seen anything that he's done to reach out to Democrats or help or anything else in that regard," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said when asked if Democrats would reach out to Musk to work together. He continued, "What he's done is destroy the State Department [and] destroy diplomacy." THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., urged Democrats to not make oversight investigations the center of their party’s agenda over the next two years with a majority in both the House and the Senate. He said the upcoming years should be focused on "leveraging this majority" to bring results to Americans. "I think there will obviously be some degree of oversight into what happened with DOGE, and I think rightfully so," Figures said. "But I don't believe that sort of oversight can become the North Star of what the party is all about over the next two years." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who was just elected by his party to serve as speaker of the House, also recently left the door open to potential investigations into Musk when asked by Fox News Digital about the conversations surrounding oversight. He deferred leaving investigation decisions up to Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — the party’s expected leaders of oversight work. The Republicans whom Fox News Digital spoke with were not totally convinced that Musk’s recent comments meant he was backing out of supporting Republicans. "I think Musk is about fiscal responsibility," Rep. Glenn Grothman, R-Wis., said. "And the Republican Party, while it lets you down some of the time, is still the party of fiscal responsibility." JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER' Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., acknowledged that Republicans in Congress "fell short," excusing the American people for being upset with her party. "It's totally in his hands, whether he supports [Republicans] or not," Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., said. "But I don't think that there's any question that this Congress fell short, specifically the Senate, and people have a right to be angry. Hell, I'm angry." Fox News Digital's request for comment from Musk was not immediately returned.

articles.title: States rally behind Catholic church in first-of-its-kind Supreme Court fight over prayer shrine
articles.summary: A Kentucky Catholic community's Virgin Mary prayer grotto sparked a neighbors' zoning fight now at the Supreme Court in a RLUIPA religious liberty case.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Catholic religious community's plans to build a small shrine to the Virgin Mary on its own property have triggered a years-long legal battle with two neighbors, drawing a coalition of state attorneys general into a potential landmark religious liberty showdown before the U.S. Supreme Court. Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman is leading an 18-state coalition urging the justices to reverse a ruling that blocked the roughly 600-square-foot prayer grotto in Park Hills, Kentucky, despite the project initially receiving approval from local zoning officials. The dispute pits the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist against neighboring property owners Joel and Elizabeth Frederic, who challenged the city's approval of the outdoor shrine and ultimately prevailed in Kentucky's appellate courts. YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE "I’m proud to stand with other Attorney General colleagues from across the country in defense of these Kentuckians’ religious liberty," Coleman said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "This fundamental American freedom cannot be brushed away simply by a heckler’s veto, and I’m confident the justices will agree." The coalition's intervention comes as the Supreme Court prepares to consider whether blocking a religious structure on an organization's property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA). The case marks the first time the Supreme Court is considering the federal law's land-use protections, according to Coleman's office, raising the stakes for churches and religious organizations nationwide. The controversy began in 2021 when the Missionaries sought permission to construct a 16-by-39-foot grotto honoring the Virgin Mary's apparition to Saint Bernadette in Lourdes, France. SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING The proposed structure would include a shrine, plaza, walking path and retaining wall, offering a quiet place for prayer and meditation. The church building has stood on the property for nearly a century, predating Park Hills' zoning ordinance adopted in 1974, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. The Park Hills Board of Adjustment approved the project in April 2021. But the Frederics challenged the approval in court, arguing that the proposed construction violated local zoning requirements. A trial court initially upheld the city's decision before the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the zoning board exceeded its authority in granting the necessary permits. SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CATHOLIC PARISH'S CHALLENGE AFTER COLORADO BARRED SCHOOLS FROM UNIVERSAL PRE-K PROGRAM The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed the rejection of the Missionaries' federal religious land-use claim in December 2025. Coleman previously defended the religious organization's position before Kentucky's highest court and led a 20-state effort in April urging the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the dispute. The justices agreed in October to hear the case, with oral arguments scheduled for Jan. 20, 2027. Ryan Gardner, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, which represents the Missionaries, previously told Fox News Digital that the stakes extend far beyond the proposed Catholic shrine. "This is a massive case for religious liberty because it has the potential to impact every single zoning law in this country," Gardner said in an October Fox News Digital exclusive. Gardner compared the grotto's footprint to a swimming pool, underscoring the modest size of a project that has since reached the nation's highest court. "RLUIPA is at the intersection of two very critical rights in this country: the rights of religious liberty and property rights," Gardner said. Congress enacted RLUIPA in 2000 to protect religious institutions from certain burdens imposed through zoning and land-use regulations. The Missionaries argue that preventing them from constructing a religious structure on their property substantially burdens their religious exercise. The Frederics, however, have disputed that interpretation, arguing in their Supreme Court opposition brief that the religious organization failed to demonstrate why alternative locations for the grotto were unavailable. They also challenged claims that lower courts are fundamentally divided over the legal standard for determining substantial burdens under RLUIPA. The Supreme Court agreed to consider the substantial-burden question, rather than every issue raised in the underlying zoning dispute. Kentucky Solicitor General Matt Kuhn, Principal Deputy Solicitor General Jack Heyburn and Deputy Solicitor General Jacob Abrahamson prepared the multistate brief, according to Coleman's office. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What began as a proposal for a quiet place to pray has become a national battle over religious liberty, property rights and how far neighbors can go in challenging religious construction on private property.

articles.title: Dem lawmaker to resign after report says he made 'unwelcome' sexual advances toward staffer
articles.summary: The House Ethics Committee says Rep. Jimmy Gomez's advances toward a House staffer could implicate D.C. laws on criminal sexual assault, its report claims.
articles.body: A West Coast Democrat announced his resignation from the House of Representatives after their bipartisan internal watchdog stated that he could have committed criminal sexual assault against congressional staffers on multiple occasions. An explosive report by the House Ethics Committee released on Monday claimed that Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., violated congressional rules on sexual misconduct by making "unwelcome" advances toward a staffer for the House, disregarding the power imbalance between lawmakers and aides in the process. The report also went a step further, warning Gomez could have violated existing law. Gomez has since announced his intent to resign on Dec. 1. HOUSE DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATED OVER ALLEGED 'INAPPROPRIATE SEXUAL CONTACT' WITH STAFFER The bipartisan panel found that "Representative Gomez knew or had reason to know that his contact was not welcome" when out with the staffer, called "Witness 1," at a D.C. bar. "There is also evidence that he knew or had reason to know his repeated advance towards Witness 1 in his congressional office was inappropriate and unwelcome. Accordingly, Representative Gomez’s conduct towards Witness 1 could implicate D.C. laws related to criminal sexual assault, including misdemeanor sexual abuse," the report said. SWALWELL ANNOUNCES RESIGNATION FROM CONGRESS AFTER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS TORPEDOED GUBERNATORIAL BID Gomez has not been charged with any crime and has maintained his innocence. Fox News Digital reached out to his office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Gomez was a close ally of disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., who resigned after being accused of sexual assault — which he denied. Gomez is also founder of the pro-family Congressional Dads Caucus. The bipartisan ethics panel announced in August that it was investigating Gomez over allegations including "inappropriate sexual contact with a House staffer." Gomez told Fox News Digital at the time that he "made personal mistakes outside my marriage" but added that his extramarital relations were consensual and that he did not break any laws. CAPITOL HILL SEX SCANDALS TRIGGER NEW PUSH TO REDRAW THE LINE FOR LAWMAKERS But the lawyers for one of the women interviewed by the committee disputed that in comments to Fox News Digital, accusing the congressman of sexual assault. Monday’s report shows the committee appears to support her side of the story, and that Gomez’s actions "at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong." The staffer is identified as having worked for a congressional leadership office, rather than on Gomez’s own staff. Before coming out with her accusations, the staffer testified to the committee that she did not want Gomez "to feel upset in any way," and that she was "afraid that I was going to get in trouble at work," the report said. "Even if Representative Gomez believed that his actions were wholly consensual, his failure to appreciate the reality of this power dynamic and thus the untenable position he put a young congressional staffer in, is inconsistent with the standards required of a Member of Congress," the report said. The investigation into Gomez began after reports surfaced that he had been seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party attended by lawmakers and House employees. Gomez initially disclosed two relationships involving congressional staffers, describing one as a past consensual sexual relationship and the other as "one sole occasion" of "consensual kissing." GOP LAWMAKER'S GIFTS, 'EFFUSIVE AFFECTION' TOWARD YOUNG STAFFERS DETAILED IN EXPLOSIVE ETHICS REPORT However, investigators found credible allegations that Gomez made unwanted sexual advances more than once toward the second woman, Witness 1, which the woman claimed was "nonconsensual whatsoever." The woman, who was in her mid-20s at the time, testified that Gomez put his hand underneath her skirt and penetrated her with his fingers without consent during a February 2024 gathering at a bar in D.C., and testified to investigators that she fled to the bathroom crying after the incident. Gomez defended himself against the allegation, telling the committee that the woman "did not say no," and did not "push" him away, while denying penetrating her. Investigators described a second encounter with the woman in July 2024, claiming that Gomez grabbed her as she attempted to leave his congressional office, pulled her toward him and tried to kiss her. She described Gomez as "[p]retty forceful" and said she repeatedly tried to push him away, the report said. Gomez denied the allegation, maintaining that he merely hugged the woman and kissed her on the cheek. Investigators then refuted his defense after they examined text messages suggesting Gomez was concerned about being seen with the woman by members of his staff, noting that he switched their communications to Signal and enabled disappearing messages. The committee also noted that Gomez initially disclosed only consensual kissing before later acknowledging sexual contact during his testimony. After reviewing documents and speaking with 10 witnesses, the committee concluded that Gomez violated clauses 1 and 18(b) of the House Code of Official Conduct, which prohibit unwelcome sexual advances toward House employees and require lawmakers to conduct themselves in a manner reflecting creditably on the House. Investigators concluded that Gomez's conduct caused the woman significant emotional distress and contributed to her decision to leave congressional employment in 2025. "The Committee reiterates its commitment to investigating allegations and providing accountability to those who face sexual misconduct from Members and their staff. Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez’s misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the report said. articles.title: Federal appeals court gives President Donald Trump a path to erasing hush money conviction
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court on Monday gave President Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, reviving his bid t...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court on Monday gave President Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, reviving his bid to move the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds.

A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals once again sent the case to a lower federal court, ordering a judge to promptly rule on Trump's request to move the historic case from state court, where he was tried and convicted.

A ruling in Trump's favor would set off a legal merry-go-round, returning the case to the 2nd Circuit where he could argue that the verdict should be discarded because of presidential immunity. Trump's lawyers have made such arguments before in various courts, but this time they'd be doing so in a forum that has now sided with him twice in his quest for federal court intervention.

A lower federal court judge, the late Alvin Hellerstein, had repeatedly denied Trump's requests to move the historic case from state court, most recently in August. The 2nd Circuit panel ruled that Hellerstein, who died in October at 92, had erred.

The decision Monday also set in motion a halt to proceedings in Trump's simultaneous state court appeal of his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels , whose affair allegations had threatened to upend his 2016 presidential campaign .

Trump denies her claim and said he did nothing wrong. The May 2024 verdict made him the first U.S. president to be convicted of a crime. He was given no punishment.

Trump's lawyers laud 'prompt and correct' ruling

The ruling came a week after 2nd Circuit Judges Raymond J. Lohier Jr., John M. Walker Jr. and José A. Cabranes spent more than an hour questioning Trump's lawyer and a state prosecutor on the matter.

Lohier and Cabranes were appointed by Democrats. Walker was appointed by a Republican.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Trump's legal team said the president "appreciates the 2nd Circuit's prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System."

The Manhattan District Attorney's Office, which prosecuted the case, declined to comment.

Trump's lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., had urged the judges to rule swiftly, arguing that without federal court intervention, the president "will likely have to wait years" for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan DA's office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein's ruling and leave the case in state court.

Trump fought conviction in state and federal courts

Along with his federal court fight, Trump has been waging a traditional appeal through New York's state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule and could be prevented from doing so indefinitely under Monday's ruling.

Giuffra sent a letter to the Appellate Division on Monday notifying that court of the 2nd Circuit ruling, including its request "that no further proceedings occur in the state courts" while jurisdiction is being settled.

In trying to move the hush money case to federal court, Trump's lawyers argued that federal officers, including presidents, have the right to be tried in federal court for charges arising from conduct performed while in office.

Manhattan prosecutors have said Trump's dealings with the Daniels matter broke state laws and weren't part of his official duties.

Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time.

Hellerstein wrote in his decision that "paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity."

Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court's July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can't be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can't use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.

Appeals court had previously sided with Trump

After Trump appealed Hellerstein's second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh "important issues relevant" to the president's request to move the case.

That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.

Giuffra told the 2nd Circuit panel last week that prosecutors at Trump's trial had used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court's immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts.

Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution's description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court.

articles.title: Fury in Congress over Huang's reinstatement as lawmakers move forward with hearings
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board's surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board's surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at the behest of President Donald Trump , opening a new phase of questions about the chipmaking giant and potential national security lapses.

Sen. Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang will testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, said the Trump administration needs to explain what role U.S. officials played in what she called a "reckless" decision.

Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's direct involvement with Nvidia's decision-making "raises serious national security and corruption questions."

"We must investigate these actions," said Garcia of California.

Nvidia was already facing sharp scrutiny from Congress after Huang acknowledged a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy. Putting Huang back in charge, after Trump said the board did "what we wanted them to do," raised stark concerns over the administration's role in the company that is central to the AI economy .

As Democrats prepare to take charge of Congress in January, they are mounting investigations into the Trump administration, particularly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has close ties with the company. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed, the company whose CEO, Alice Huang, was involved with Jensen Huang.

"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," said Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.

"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

Huang is expected to appear for two days of interviews with three House committees next week, along with his public hearing at the Senate panel.

"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," said a joint statement from Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on China; Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., chairman of the House Intelligence Committee; and Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary's AI capabilities."

Of concern to Congress is whether Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, has been selling its chips to China, in violation of export controls as the U.S. tries to protect certain technology that is at the core of the AI race.

Earlier this year, members of Congress urged the U.S. Commerce Department to "suspend or reconsider" Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full national security review, according to a release earlier this month from Warren and a key Republican on the Senate banking committee, Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana.

"Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China's military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.," they wrote in a statement in November.

"NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer," the two senators said.

Republicans and Democrats are demanding answers

While Republican leaders were mostly quiet on Huang's return to Nvidia, other Republicans spoke more forcefully Monday.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his seat after Trump endorsed his GOP primary opponent, questioned the company's comment that the U.S. said there was no security risk.

"No national security risk? Based on what?" Cornyn posted. Cornyn asked whether the FBI did a defensive briefing of Huang to conclude there was no risk, "If not, why not?"

Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon wrote on social media that the U.S. cannot say it wants to win the AI competition and then give China its best technology. "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," wrote Bacon, who is retiring from Congress.

Ahead of the announcement but after Trump's call for Huang to be reinstated, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who lost reelection to a Democrat, posted: "Ummm… she was, and is, a spy. How about we get serious about making sure China doesn't steal US company technology?"

Utah Sen. John Curtis asked similar questions.

"Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?" Curtis asked. "And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"

Democrats add to their anti-corruption agenda

Democrats are preparing to dive more deeply into questions of national security and political corruption in Washington as they take over the committee gavels in January.

"The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?" posted Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to become the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when Democrats take the majority.

Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, said that Congress should investigate "what stock positions took place before the announcement."

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who will chair the Senate finance committee and serves on the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang's restatement shows that under Trump and his administration, "our national security is for sale."

"In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable," Wyden said.

Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Aamer Madhani, Joey Cappelletti and Chris Rugaber contributed to this report.
