articles.title: Bessent gave Iran weeks before it had ‘nothing left to trade.’ New sanctions expose what survived
articles.summary: Scott Bessent warned Iran had two weeks. Two months later, Treasury hit over two dozen entities in Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey moving billions for Tehran.
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in September that Iran would have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks. Nearly two months later, the Trump administration is still targeting the overseas financial networks Tehran has used to keep money moving despite sweeping U.S. sanctions in the midst of ongoing war. On Monday, Treasury announced another round of sanctions targeting more than two dozen individuals and companies accused of helping Iran move billions of dollars through financial networks spanning Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey. Bessent has repeatedly warned that Iran is nearing economic collapse, describing successive crackdowns as steps toward cutting off the regime's remaining financial lifelines. Yet each new round of sanctions has exposed more of the networks Tehran has used to keep doing business abroad — even as mounting economic pressure has failed to produce a diplomatic breakthrough. COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES While the administration says its blockade has largely stopped Iranian oil exports, Monday's sanctions detail how Tehran has relied on currency dealers, trading companies and middlemen to conduct business abroad. Treasury identified approximately $14.7 billion in financial activity potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking between January 2025 and August 2026, underscoring the scale of the networks Washington is now targeting. Just three days earlier, Treasury declared that Iran had exhausted its seaborne oil supply outside the U.S. blockade, saying no new oil had been loaded onto vessels since the launch of Operation Economic Outcast in August. "The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking," Bessent said Friday. In a response to Fox News Digital, Treasury said Iran has not loaded a single barrel of oil onto vessels since Aug. 25, 2026, and claimed Tehran is struggling to access foreign currency and recover proceeds from previous oil sales. The department also provided a report showing the Iranian rial has lost roughly 25% of its value since August, while inflation reached 90% in September. Treasury said it is continuing to target alternative financial channels, including cryptocurrency exchanges, as Tehran looks for ways around U.S. restrictions. BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP But even as the administration claims success in cutting off new oil shipments, Treasury is still pursuing Iranian operatives accused of collecting billions of dollars from previous sales. Friday's sanctions targeted four individuals involved in recovering oil revenues held overseas, some of which Treasury said had been diverted by middlemen for personal gain. Bessent's September prediction was hardly his first warning that Tehran was approaching an economic breaking point. Months earlier, he said U.S. sanctions were "asphyxiating" Iran's economy and warned that the country could soon be forced to shut down oil wells as storage facilities filled up. By late August, Bessent was predicting Iran's economy could collapse within "weeks or months," as the administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign aimed at cutting off the regime's remaining revenue. The warnings continued in October, when Bessent projected Iran's economy could shrink by more than 25% over the year ending in March 2027. Earlier this month, he described the country as experiencing one of the fastest economic collapses in history. BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY The administration had increasingly turned to economic pressure after months of military strikes failed to force Tehran into an agreement. Washington reimposed its naval blockade in July after an interim deal collapsed, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in September that the price Iran would pay going forward would be primarily economic, although military action remained an option. But neither the military campaign nor the mounting economic pressure has produced a broader agreement. Iran continues to demand sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and an end to the blockade, while Washington is pressing Tehran for concessions on its nuclear program and regional activities. Despite months of escalating pressure, Treasury is still identifying overseas financial networks that have allowed Iran to conduct business outside traditional banking channels. Iran has spent decades developing ways around American financial restrictions, relying on middlemen, shell companies and foreign currency exchanges to keep trade flowing even as Washington moves to cut off its access to international markets. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Monday's announcement detailed some of those channels, including exchange houses and trading companies operating across Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong. Among the newly sanctioned entities was an Iranian currency exchange center that Treasury says facilitates tens of billions of dollars in annual trade, connecting exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to purchase goods abroad.

articles.title: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez to resign from Congress after evidence of sexual misconduct
articles.summary: Jimmy Gomez, who lost his election this month and only serving in the House until the year's end, was accused of sexual misconduct with a staff member.
articles.body:
US Representative Jimmy Gomez has said he will resign from Congress after an ethics committee said it found credible evidence that he engaged in sexual misconduct, according to CBS News.

A report released on Monday by the House Ethics Committee stated that Gomez, a California Democrat, made "unwelcome sexual advances" towards a House staff member, "disregarding the power imbalance" between them.

Gomez, 51, said he disagreed with the report's findings but would resign on 1 December. The five-term congressman lost his seat representing part of Los Angeles in the midterm elections this month and was set to leave the House at the end of the year.

The BBC has contacted Gomez's office for comment.

Gomez said in a statement on Monday that he had "strong disagreements" with the committee's findings, but that he saw "no other alternative than to resign", according to CBS, the BBC's US media partner.

He added: "I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage."

The panel originally investigated a report that Gomez had been seen kissing a younger staffer at a party hosted by then-Congressman Eric Swalwell. That report came shortly after Swalwell, also a California Democrat, resigned over sexual misconduct allegations of his own.

The bipartisan committee announced its investigation into Gomez, who is married, in August, after lawyers for the House staffer accused him of inappropriate sexual contact. He had maintained at the time that while he had made mistakes, his actions were consensual.

The ethics committee interviewed a woman, referred to only as "Witness 1" in the report, who said the congressman made unwanted sexual advances toward her on two occasions, once in public and once in his congressional office, while she was a House staffer.

She alleged Gomez "put his hand down my skirt" while they were at a bar in Washington DC in February 2024, describing the incident as "nonconsensual whatsoever".

Gomez's conduct caused the House staffer "significant and ongoing distress", contributing to her decision to leave her job, according to the report.

The woman's attorneys, Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, said in a statement on Monday that Gomez "abused the power given to him by the voters" and that in his actions "he was effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public service".

While they applauded the report, the attorneys said Gomez's conduct "did not occur in a vacuum", calling for immediate steps by Congress to "rein in what the report describes as a 'toxic and predatory culture'".

The committee said in its report on Monday that it did not have enough time "to pursue an adequate House sanction" against Gomez as he is set to leave Congress next month.

The House Ethics Committee last week approved changes to how the bipartisan panel handles sexual misconduct investigations, including ways to speed up its inquiries.

Gomez lost to Angela Gonzales-Torres, also a Democrat, in this month's election by some 25 percentage points after a campaign in which the sexual misconduct investigation became a focal point.

articles.body: Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha aprovechado su entrevista con Carlos Franganillo en 'Informativos Telecinco' para desgranar algunas de las principales propuestas del Partido Popular (PP) y fijar su posición sobre cuestiones como la Ley de Amnistía, los posibles pactos con Vox, la inmigración, la vivienda y las pensiones. El líder de los populares ha reiterado su compromiso de derogar la norma que benefició a los encausados por el procés independentista y ha asegurado que respetará el resultado de las urnas a la hora de abordar los acuerdos políticos necesarios para gobernar. "El Tribunal Supremo ha dictado esa sentencia, ha sido respetuoso con el Constitucional, pero yo derogaré la Ley de Amnistía", ha afirmado Núñez Feijóo al ser preguntado por la posibilidad de sentarse en el futuro con Carles Puigdemont. El dirigente popular ha recordado que el PP pudo haber contado con los votos de Junts para alcanzar la presidencia del Gobierno en 2023, pero ha defendido que "no todo vale en política". "No estoy dispuesto a hacer cualquier cosa para ser presidente del Gobierno", ha añadido, antes de insistir en que ningún político debe tener más derechos que el resto de los ciudadanos ni capacidad para modificar el Código Penal en su propio beneficio. Sobre los posibles acuerdos con Vox, Núñez Feijóo ha evitado anticipar las condiciones de una futura negociación, aunque ha asegurado que respetará la voluntad de los votantes. "Si Vox sigue siendo la tercera fuerza, y parece que lo es, y además va a sacar buenos resultados, y más de cuatro millones de ciudadanos les van a votar, yo respetaré el resultado de las urnas", ha señalado. En cualquier caso, ha descartado expresamente cualquier entendimiento con EH Bildu: "Yo no pactaré con Bildu, eso lo aseguro". El presidente del PP también ha defendido los acuerdos alcanzados con Vox en distintas comunidades autónomas, frente a los recelos que suscitan entre parte del electorado. A su juicio, se trata de pactos públicos y transparentes, que ha contrapuesto a los acuerdos del Gobierno con la formación abertzale. "Lo que hemos pactado con Vox no es un pacto encapuchado como el de Bildu. Es un pacto con luz y taquígrafos y nosotros respetaremos ese pacto", ha manifestado. Preguntado por el concepto de "prioridad nacional" incluido en los acuerdos con Vox, Núñez Feijóo ha defendido que lo importante no es tanto la denominación como las medidas concretas que recoge. Según ha explicado, el criterio pactado contempla establecer un sistema de baremación para acceder a las ayudas públicas que tenga en cuenta factores como el tiempo de empadronamiento en una comunidad autónoma, el historial de residencia en España y la renta de los solicitantes. "La prioridad nacional que nosotros hemos pactado, porque lo importante no es lo que se dice, sino lo que se hace, es dar información, dar un sistema para las ayudas públicas con un baremo", ha señalado. Al ser preguntado por qué no se había utilizado el término "prioridad de arraigo" si la intención era reconocer el tiempo de vinculación con un territorio, el líder del PP ha asegurado que lo determinante es el contenido de los acuerdos y su adecuación al ordenamiento jurídico. En este sentido, ha establecido dos límites legales a una interpretación extrema de la prioridad nacional: "La Constitución española y los tratados de la UE". "Por tanto, todos los acuerdos tienen que hacerse de acuerdo con las leyes", ha subrayado. Sobre la posibilidad de que Vox convierta la prioridad nacional en una condición para facilitar su investidura, Núñez Feijóo ha insistido en que no se pueden firmar acuerdos contrarios a la legalidad. "Nadie puede firmar acuerdos ilegales", ha afirmado, antes de volver a referirse a la Ley de Amnistía y criticar la actuación del Gobierno y del Tribunal Constitucional. El dirigente popular ha asegurado que no seguirá ese camino y ha añadido que, en un eventual escenario de gobierno, "en el Constitucional no va a haber exministros del Gobierno". Preguntado por las posibles líneas rojas e ирrenunciables de cara a un futuro acuerdo de investidura con Vox, Núñez Feijóo ha situado el cumplimiento de la legalidad como condición fundamental. "Quiero ser presidente del Gobierno de un Estado de derecho", ha afirmado. Entre los principios que considera intocables ha mencionado las leyes de igualdad para combatir el machismo y los derechos del colectivo LGTBI. "Todo esto ya lo hemos discutido. Todo esto está en los acuerdos de las comunidades autónomas. Y están cumpliendo", ha asegurado. El líder del PP también ha vuelto a referirse al arraigo como criterio para establecer la prioridad en el acceso a determinadas ayudas y ha insistido en que no está dispuesto a incumplir el ordenamiento jurídico. "Las leyes de mi país tienen una por encima de todas, que es la Constitución. Lo que no cabe en la Constitución yo no lo voy a negociar", ha sentenciado. La política migratoria ha ocupado buena parte de la conversación. Núñez Feijóo ha defendido un modelo basado en la llegada de trabajadores extranjeros cuando exista demanda de mano de obra y ha resumido su planteamiento con una frase: "Inmigración ordenada y para trabajar, cuando la necesitemos; descontrol migratorio, no". En este sentido, ha asegurado que los extranjeros que residan legalmente en España, trabajen y cumplan las leyes no tendrán dificultades para permanecer en el país. "Los que están trabajando legalmente, residen legalmente y cumplen las leyes, no tienen ninguna dificultad para quedarse", ha afirmado. Por el contrario, ha defendido que las personas que entren de manera irregular deben retornar a sus países de origen y ha cuestionado la política migratoria del Ejecutivo, especialmente por la regularización extraordinaria de inmigrantes. Preguntado por la falta de trabajadores en el sector de la construcción y la necesidad de mano de obra para desarrollar su plan de vivienda, el dirigente popular ha apuntado que existe una bolsa de desempleados que podría incorporarse a esta actividad. También ha defendido la contratación de trabajadores extranjeros mediante ofertas laborales y permisos de residencia. "Hay muchos extranjeros que no trabajan en la construcción porque no hay construcción", ha argumentado. Núñez Feijóo ha insistido en que las empresas podrán contratar a trabajadores de otros países cuando dispongan de un contrato de trabajo, y ha citado expresamente a ciudadanos peruanos y colombianos como posibles profesionales para cubrir esas necesidades. Asimismo, ha defendido que la inmigración regular debe conservar sus derechos, pero siempre vinculados al cumplimiento de las obligaciones legales. La vivienda ha sido otro de los ejes centrales de la entrevista. Núñez Feijóo ha reiterado su propuesta de impulsar la construcción de un millón de viviendas, con una media de 250.000 nuevas unidades al año, frente a las aproximadamente 600.000 que, según ha recordado, se llegaron a construir anualmente en España durante los años de la burbuja inmobiliaria. El líder del PP ha planteado poner suelo público a disposición de los promotores, aprovechar los terrenos de la Sareb y facilitar la colaboración entre administraciones para incrementar la oferta. También ha defendido destinar los remanentes presupuestarios de los ayuntamientos a vivienda pública y protegida. En su opinión, la disponibilidad de suelo a menor coste podría contribuir a reducir entre un 35% y un 40% el precio de las viviendas construidas sobre esos terrenos. Entre las medidas que propone figuran también una reforma de la legislación urbanística, la agilización de las licencias y una ley contra la ocupación ilegal. Núñez Feijóo ha defendido que los ayuntamientos dispongan de un plazo de 90 días para conceder las licencias y que, si no lo hacen, pueda iniciarse la obra mediante una declaración responsable, siempre que se cumpla la normativa urbanística. "El problema es que no hay vivienda", ha resumido. En materia de pensiones, Núñez Feijóo ha reiterado que, si llega al Gobierno, las revalorizará conforme al IPC. "Voy a revalorizar las pensiones conforme al IPC sí o sí", ha asegurado. No obstante, ha advertido de los desafíos que plantea el envejecimiento de la población y ha defendido la necesidad de aumentar el número de cotizantes mediante el crecimiento económico y la creación de empleo. Como ejemplo, ha relacionado su plan de construcción de un millón de viviendas con la generación de nuevos puestos de trabajo y ha sostenido que el desarrollo de esta actividad podría contribuir a incorporar medio millón de cotizantes. También ha cuestionado el incremento de la deuda pública y del gasto del Estado durante la actual legislatura, y ha defendido un modelo económico basado en la inversión privada y extranjera. Por otro lado, el dirigente popular ha avanzado que su eventual Gobierno realizará una auditoría de las cuentas públicas, ante la falta de presupuestos generales durante los últimos tres años. "Estamos en una habitación oscura, porque llevamos tres años sin presupuesto", ha afirmado. Núñez Feijóo no ha descartado encontrar situaciones económicas que no se hayan previsto y ha defendido una bajada selectiva de impuestos como fórmula para estimular la actividad y el empleo sin reducir necesariamente la recaudación. Durante la entrevista, también ha cuestionado la gestión del Ejecutivo en educación y sanidad, ha aludido a los resultados del informe PISA y ha defendido que España necesita recuperar la confianza de los inversores. Su planteamiento, ha insistido, pasa por impulsar una economía que crezca de manera sostenible y permita garantizar tanto los servicios públicos como el sistema de pensiones. La gestión de la DANA en la Comunidad Valenciana y la posterior dimisión de Carlos Mazón también han tenido espacio en la entrevista. Feijóo ha asegurado que aconsejó al entonces presidente valenciano que solicitara la declaración de emergencia nacional y ha criticado su actuación durante la tragedia. "Yo le aconsejé a Carlos Mazón que pidiera la emergencia nacional. Porque sorprendentemente el presidente quería escaquearse, y se escaqueó", ha afirmado. El líder del PP ha considerado que la imagen de Carlos Mazón abandonando Paiporta durante la visita de los Reyes y del presidente del Gobierno fue también "la imagen huyendo de la gestión de la DANA". Núñez Feijóo ha explicado que aquella mañana se encontraba en el pleno del Congreso y que llegó a plantearse la suspensión de la sesión por la gravedad de las consecuencias de las inundaciones. También ha cuestionado que, después de suspenderse el pleno, se convocara otro extraordinario para abordar el nombramiento del consejo de administración de RTVE. En este contexto, ha asegurado que, si se encontrara ante una catástrofe similar como presidente del Gobierno, asumiría las responsabilidades que implica el cargo. "Si me vuelve a pasar lo de la DANA en algún lugar, asumiré la responsabilidad que supone ser presidente del Gobierno", ha señalado. Sobre Carlos Mazón, ha reconocido que se equivocó al no pedir la emergencia nacional y ha recordado que el expresidente valenciano cesó a dos miembros de su Gobierno durante los primeros días de la crisis, permaneció al frente de la gestión y finalmente dimitió un año después. "Imagine un país asumiendo cada uno su responsabilidad", ha añadido. Preguntado por la posibilidad de que Carlos Mazón continúe como diputado autonómico o forme parte de las próximas listas electorales del PP en la Comunidad Valenciana, Núñez Feijóo ha asegurado que todavía no ha abordado esa cuestión. "Lo que tengo planteado es que quiero ganar las elecciones y que quiero volver a gobernar en Valencia. Pero las listas de la Comunitat ni las hemos hablado ni las hemos comentado", ha respondido. El presidente del PP ha aprovechado también para cuestionar la ausencia de dimisiones en otras crisis recientes, como los problemas ferroviarios, el apagón eléctrico o la situación en Ceuta. En particular, ha aludido al ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, y a la actitud de Pedro Sánchez tras el funeral de Estado por las víctimas de la DANA. "¿Me puede decir alguien que haya dimitido? Salvo el señor Puente", ha preguntado, antes de criticar que el presidente del Gobierno participara en actos electorales poco después del homenaje a las víctimas.

articles.title: Former Navy SEAL says New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill puts protected speech in the crosshairs
articles.summary: A former Navy SEAL and lawyer warns that New Jersey's Assembly Bill 1146 could function as a "backdoor blasphemy law" chilling public debate.
articles.body: A New Jersey proposal aimed at combating anti-Muslim discrimination could make Americans think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas, a lawyer and former Navy SEAL warned. Bill Brown, a partner at Parlatore Law Group, told Fox News Digital that Assembly Bill 1146 contains language broad enough to discourage public debate, even though the legislation expressly preserves First Amendment rights. "The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate," Brown said. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS The proposal would establish a state definition of Islamophobia and require public officials and law enforcement officers to consider it when determining whether alleged discriminatory acts were motivated by anti-Muslim bias. Brown argued that requiring officials to use a definition that includes harsh criticism and other speech could make people afraid to speak openly. CHRISTIAN GROUPS AND PASTORS SAY NEW CALIFORNIA LGBT HATE SPEECH LAW IS DISGUISED AS INDOCTRINATION "The First Amendment guarantees that no religion or theology is immune to criticism," he said. Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen sponsors the bill, which is co-sponsored by fellow Democrats Assemblywomen Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Mitchelle Drulis and Assemblyman Roy Freiman. The legislation describes a uniform definition as a tool to help officials identify and investigate anti-Muslim crime, harassment and discrimination." Fox News Digital made multiple attempts to contact Danielsen and all three co-sponsors for comment but did not receive a response. Its definition includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture," as well as "rhetorical, violent, or physical anti-Muslim manifestations." Other examples include pulling hijabs from Muslim women, discriminatory treatment and blaming Muslims collectively for wrongdoing committed by an individual or group. CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS The bill would create no standalone criminal offense for criticizing Islam. It directs officials to consider the definition when reviewing an alleged violation of an existing policy, law or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts. It also explicitly says nothing in the legislation should diminish or infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment or New Jersey’s Constitution. AMERICA'S FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR EXPOSES A POLITICAL BLIND SPOT Asked about that safeguard, Brown maintained that the prospect of scrutiny itself could discourage people from speaking, regardless of whether a case ultimately succeeds. He also singled out a provision in the bill’s legislative findings that lists "anti-Islamism" among terms that may describe the same characteristics as Islamophobia. Brown argued that the wording risks blurring the distinction between prejudice against Muslim people and criticism of a political movement. JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH "Islamism is a distinct geopolitical movement," he said. "It’s not just a religious faith." Brown described the proposal as a "backdoor blasphemy law," arguing that government should protect people’s rights while allowing their religious beliefs to face public scrutiny. PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH' The legislation excludes criticism of Muslim-majority countries comparable to criticism directed at other countries. Brown argued that criticism of religious and political ideology also needs protection. Brown said his concerns are informed in part by his military service. He recalled responding to two suicide bombings in Iraq and said he remains committed to speaking out against jihadist ideology. He also recalled studying Arabic at Rutgers after leaving the military, where Muslim American classmates helped him when he struggled with the language. For Brown, the broader concern is whether Americans will feel free to challenge ideas they oppose. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "True diversity is diversity of thought," he said.

articles.title: Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after Ethics Committee finds he engaged in sexual misconduct
articles.summary: Gomez — who lost his re-election bid this month — said that while he cooperated with the investigation, he had “strong disagreements” with the committee’s conclusions.
articles.body: Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., said Monday he will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found that he engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer and said that his behavior could constitute “criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.” “I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report, and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” Gomez said in a statement. He said he cooperated with the Ethics investigation but added he has “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” “Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred,” Gomez said in his statement. “I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond. “With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs,” he said. His resignation will speed up his departure from Congress by about one month. Earlier this month, Democratic socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres defeated Gomez in California’s 34th District, as he faced the ethics investigation. The development comes months after Gomez’s close friend, former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., dropped his bid for governor and resigned from office following sexual assault allegations from multiple women, including a House staffer. The Ethics panel had launched an investigation into Gomez in the wake of the Swalwell saga after news reports that the married Gomez was observed at a party kissing a House staffer. Gomez disclosed to the Ethics panel he had interactions with two women, including “consensual kissing.” But one of the women, identified as “Witness 1” in the new Ethics report, described the interactions with Gomez as unwanted sexual advances. Witness 1 was in her mid-20s and worked for a House leadership office and not for Gomez, according to the committee. She left her job as a House staffer in 2025. During the first incident, while celebrating an unidentified member of Congress’ birthday in 2024, the woman told the committee that Gomez groped and sexually assaulted her at Rocket Bar in Washington, D.C., according to the report. When they went outside, she told investigators he pushed her against the wall and began kissing her. The congressman told the committee that he did kiss the woman outside the bar and that there was sexual contact but that she gave him consent. Witness 1 later told another person her account, that second witness told investigators. During a second incident, Witness 1 said she went to Gomez’s congressional office during late votes and that he tried to kiss her and was “forceful” with her; she said his actions were nonconsensual, according to the report. Gomez, speaking to the Ethics panel, rejected that characterization and said there was no indication she was uncomfortable and that he did not try to prevent her from leaving. The Ethics panel did not issue a recommendation for the full House, such as censure or expulsion, presumably because Gomez was slated to leave Congress in January. But the panel said it issued its report as a warning to the entire House of Representatives. “There must be zero tolerance for unwanted sexual advances toward House staff. The Committee is tasked with investigating alleged misconduct and, where appropriate, holding Members accountable for conduct that does not reflect creditably on the House or puts other Members and staff in danger,” the Ethics panel wrote in its report. “Having determined that Representative Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward a House staffer, the Committee adopted this Report to hold Representative Gomez accountable and to serve as a warning to the entire House community that this conduct will not be tolerated,” the committee added. Responding to Gomez’s resignation, the top three House Democrats, Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, said in a joint statement: “The report of wrongdoing and abuse of power by Rep. Gomez is serious and deeply troubling. It is appropriate that he is stepping down. Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats.” The Gomez report comes just days after the Ethics Committee formally adopted six changes to its procedures aimed at speeding up investigations and increasing transparency, particularly in cases involving sexual misconduct. All six proposed changes were adopted without amendment following a rare public meeting, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to NBC News. The changes include formally requiring public disclosure of substantiated sexual misconduct findings while protecting victims’ identities; allowing the chairman and ranking member to jointly issue subpoenas without a full committee vote; and streamlining disciplinary proceedings. The reforms follow longstanding scrutiny over the pace and secrecy of congressional misconduct investigations, including cases in which lawmakers resign before investigations conclude. The changes come amid a separate bipartisan congressional workplace reform effort announced earlier this year. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Ethics panel, said the reforms followed bipartisan deliberations and collaboration with the Congressional Women’s Caucus. “The House of Representatives must have a zero-tolerance policy for sexual harassment and misconduct and the Committee on Ethics is committed to ensuring that its practices and processes sufficiently hold perpetrators accountable and deliver justice for survivors,” DeSaulnier said.

articles.title: Pepa Millán, portavoz de Vox: "El Gobierno ha dinamitado la convivencia entre españoles y ha sembrado el odio"
articles.standfirst: La portavoz de Vox carga contra el Ejecutivo de Pedro Sánchez durante el debate a ocho de RTVE, al que acusa de haber generado división y crispación, y responsabiliza a sus políticas migratorias del aumento de la inseguridad
articles.summary: La portavoz de Vox carga contra el Ejecutivo de Pedro Sánchez durante el debate a ocho de RTVE, al que acusa de haber generado división y crispación, y responsabiliza a sus políticas migratorias del aumento de la inseguridad
articles.body: El debate a ocho de RTVE ha vuelto a evidenciar la distancia entre los bloques políticos, con los reproches al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, la corrupción y la crispación como principales protagonistas de buena parte de los enfrentamientos. La portavoz del Partido Popular (PP), Ester Muñoz, ha centrado sus intervenciones en denunciar la división política y los casos de corrupción que, a su juicio, han marcado la legislatura, mientras que Pepa Millán, de Vox, ha elevado el tono contra el Ejecutivo por su gestión y sus políticas migratorias. Por su parte, Míriam Nogueras (Junts) ha reivindicado el papel de su formación en la defensa de los intereses de Cataluña y ha asegurado que volverá a ser decisiva tras las elecciones. Maribel Vaquero (PNV) ha defendido la capacidad de anticipación de su partido en materia económica y ha reivindicado el autogobierno vasco, además de descartar cualquier entendimiento con Vox. Ester Muñoz ha abierto uno de sus turnos con una crítica directa a la estrategia política del presidente del Gobierno. "Esta legislatura empezó con un presidente subido a la tribuna del Congreso diciendo que iba a construir un muro contra la mitad de los españoles. Ya sabemos lo que ha venido después. División, enfrentamiento, crispación", ha afirmado, en referencia al discurso de investidura de Pedro Sánchez de noviembre de 2023. La portavoz popular ha acusado a los partidos de izquierdas de contribuir al clima de confrontación y de guardar silencio ante determinados episodios de tensión política. En este sentido, ha recordado las declaraciones de una ministra que habló de dar "cuatro bofetadas" a Alberto Núñez Feijóo y las amenazas que, según ha denunciado, han recibido afiliados socialistas durante la campaña. "Son absolutamente cómplices del estado de crispación y de odio en el que nos encontramos en España", ha reprochado. La corrupción ha sido otro de los principales argumentos de Muñoz, que ha calificado de "sistémica" la situación durante la legislatura. La portavoz del PP ha hablado de 18 sumarios y 131 imputados y ha acusado a los partidos que sostienen al Ejecutivo de no haber reaccionado ante los distintos casos conocidos. "Todos ustedes son cómplices de cada uno de los casos de corrupción del Partido Socialista. Ustedes han preferido que Pedro Sánchez siga en La Moncloa", ha afirmado. Muñoz ha reforzado su acusación mostrando una fotografía en la que aparecían José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, Santos Cerdán, José Luis Ábalos, Leire Díez, Koldo García y el exfiscal general del Estado Álvaro García Ortiz. "Esto es lo que tenemos que cambiar el próximo 29 de noviembre. La corrupción sistémica en nuestro país, la falta de gestión, la falta de rigor, la falta de decencia", ha señalado. La representante popular también ha defendido la experiencia de gestión de Feijóo durante sus 13 años al frente de la Xunta de Galicia y ha asegurado que es posible tener un Gobierno "serio, riguroso y con decencia". La portavoz de Vox, Pepa Millán, ha dirigido buena parte de sus críticas contra el Ejecutivo y sus socios parlamentarios. En uno de los momentos más tensos del debate, ha acusado al PSOE de haber situado al "brazo político de ETA", en referencia a EH Bildu, al frente de la dirección del Estado. Millán también ha reprochado al Gobierno sus acuerdos parlamentarios y ha recuperado la negociación con Junts para cuestionar sus concesiones políticas. "Presos por presupuestos y los miembros del Gobierno, Santos Cerdán viajando a Waterloo para hacernos a todos los españoles pagar el peaje de los siete votos", ha afirmado, antes de acusar a la izquierda de promover la violencia y el estallido social. La inmigración ha centrado otro de sus ataques. Millán ha responsabilizado al Ejecutivo de generar inseguridad mediante sus "políticas de puertas abiertas" y ha vinculado la regularización de migrantes con la llegada de delitos que ha calificado de "desconocidos" en España. También ha cuestionado las políticas de protección a las mujeres del Gobierno y ha defendido la cadena perpetua para los condenados por violación. En su intervención final, la portavoz de Vox ha asegurado que el Ejecutivo ha "dinamitado la convivencia entre españoles" y "sembrado el odio". "Antes en España se trabajaba para tener un proyecto de vida y hoy para sobrevivir frente a un Gobierno absolutamente corrupto", ha afirmado. Millán ha concluido que, con Vox, los españoles "no van a volver a ser la moneda de cambio de ningún interés político". Junts reivindica su papel decisivo y el PNV marca distancias con Vox Míriam Nogueras ha defendido que Junts ha sido la formación que más ha protegido a la clase media y a los trabajadores durante la última legislatura. Como ejemplo, ha señalado que su partido votó en contra de la subida de las cuotas de los autónomos y a favor de reducir el impuesto de sociedades para pymes y cooperativas. La portavoz también ha insistido en que los recursos de Cataluña deben revertir en el territorio y ha denunciado las diferencias de inversión entre comunidades autónomas. Según las cifras que ha aportado, el Gobierno invierte 162 euros por catalán, frente a los 452 euros por madrileño y los 590 por murciano. De cara a las elecciones, Nogueras ha reivindicado la capacidad de Junts para condicionar la gobernabilidad y frenar a la derecha. "Volveremos a ser decisivos y podremos frenar a la extrema derecha", ha asegurado. Asimismo, ha defendido que su formación seguirá concentrando el voto catalán y trabajando para frenar la "decadencia" que, a su juicio, representan tanto el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez como el de Salvador Illa en Cataluña. Por su parte, Maribel Vaquero ha centrado sus intervenciones en reivindicar la autonomía del PNV y su capacidad de anticipación económica. En relación con la inflación, ha reconocido que se trata de una de las principales preocupaciones de los ciudadanos, pero ha defendido que su partido ha actuado ante los riesgos económicos. Como ejemplo, ha recordado que el PNV entregó al vicepresidente Carlos Cuerpo un documento con 31 propuestas para reducir el IVA y el precio de la electricidad tras la subida de aranceles anunciada por Donald Trump. "Esta es la forma de actuar: anticipación", ha resumido Vaquero, que también ha defendido la participación autónoma de Euskadi en competiciones deportivas internacionales, tomando como referencia la pelota vasca. "No vamos en contra de nadie, vamos a favor de Euskadi", ha afirmado. La representante nacionalista ha sido tajante al descartar cualquier acuerdo con Vox: "Con Vox no, nada, nunca". Además, ha advertido de que el PNV defenderá el concierto económico, las instituciones vascas y los derechos forales incluso en el escenario de un Gobierno de PP y Vox. En su minuto final, Ester Muñoz ha apelado a los ciudadanos que desean un cambio político y ha situado la vivienda, el coste de la vida y la situación económica entre las principales preocupaciones de los votantes. También ha recuperado las referencias a los casos de corrupción y a la gestión del Gobierno durante la legislatura. Frente a este escenario, ha prometido que un Ejecutivo del PP permitirá a los ciudadanos comprar una vivienda, llegar a final de mes con mayor facilidad y pagar menos impuestos. "El próximo 29 de noviembre, si todos los que quieren cambio votan a Alberto Núñez Feijóo, el domingo, entre todos, derribamos el muro y ponemos España en marcha", ha concluido.

articles.title: Appeals court gives Trump another chance to move his hush money conviction case to a federal venue
articles.summary: The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found a federal judge “erred” when he ruled that President Donald Trump had waited too long to raise his immunity defense.
articles.body: An appeals court on Monday opened the door to moving to federal court President Donald Trump’s New York state criminal case that resulted in a felony conviction. In a brief two-page order, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court judge had “erred” when he ruled Trump’s legal team had waited too long to raise a presidential immunity defense. “We disagree with the district court,” the three-judge panel said, directing a lower court judge to reconsider Trump’s motion to move the case from state court. U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in August had denied Trump’s request to consider moving the case, finding his arguments were not “legally sufficient.” A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team praised the appeals court’s “prompt and correct ruling.” “As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” his statement said. “President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn,” it added. A spokesperson for the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which prosecuted the case, declined to comment. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024 as part of a scheme to cover up a hush money payment that his attorney had paid to an adult film star during the 2016 presidential campaign. Trump managed the repayment to his attorney while he was president, and his lawyers have contended that a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that expanded the parameters of presidential immunity after he’d already been convicted should have resulted in the conviction being overturned. Trump, who has denied any wrongdoing, had been separately appealing the conviction in state court, but Monday’s order effectively freezes that case while it’s being decided in federal court. “In order to preserve the status quo, the district court shall also respectfully request that no further proceedings occur in the state courts while the removal question is pending,” the judges wrote. Judges Raymond Lohier, John Walker and Jose Cabranes also found that if the lower court decides the case should be moved to a federal venue, the “court should adopt the state court judgement.” That would allow Trump to make his case for the conviction to be tossed out by the 2nd Circuit. It’s unclear who will hear the case at the lower federal court level. Hellerstein died last month at age 92, and the case has yet to be reassigned. Hellerstein had previously rejected other attempts by Trump to move the case, finding “hush money paid to an adult film star is not related to a President’s official acts.” During arguments before the 2nd Circuit last week, Steven Wu of the district attorney’s office argued Trump had been prosecuted for falsifying business records, not for official presidential conduct, and that challenges to the conviction should go through the state courts. Trump attorney Robert Giuffra acknowledged to the appeals court judges last week that it was unusual for a defendant to try to move a case after he’d already been convicted, but noted, “Everything about this case is unprecedented.” Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge in the case 10 days before he was sworn in for his second term as president. The sentence meant that the conviction is on his record, but with no further penalties.

articles.title: How will voters respond to divided government?: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into how an electorate that is hungry for results may collide withe the realities of divided government.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into how an electorate that is hungry for results may collide withe the realities of divided government. Plus, we look ahead to the governor’s races on the ballot in the South next year. — Adam Wollner Which party is expected to deliver in divided government? The last 3 presidential elections provide clues. Analysis by Sahil Kapur With Democrats poised to claim historic majorities in the House and Senate come January, the biggest substantive question is what they’ll be able to accomplish with President Donald Trump in the White House over the next two years. And the biggest political question: If little is done, who will pay the price? A common theory after midterm elections is that the party that just won needs to prove it can govern — and deliver tangible results — in order to be successful in the next presidential election. But is that actually true? History says no — voters tend to punish the president’s party, not the party that captured one or both chambers of Congress in the previous midterm, when they’re unhappy with the status quo. Let’s review what happened after the last three midterms. 2014: Republicans flipped the Senate and expanded their House majority for President Barack Obama’s final two years in office. But what happened next? Not much. Congress passed 172 substantive bills (not including ceremonial ones like renaming federal buildings), according to the Pew Research Center, well below the average of 236 substantive bills over the last four decades. Highlights included a surface transportation bill, unwinding “No Child Left Behind” and a Medicare bookkeeping resolution known as the “doc fix.” There was plenty of fighting, including the rebellion that led to Speaker John Boehner’s resignation and countless Affordable Care Act repeal show votes. So, did voters punish Republicans? No. They won the trifecta in 2016, with Trump becoming president for the first time. 2018: Two years later, Democrats flipped about 40 House seats and took control of the chamber, although Republicans kept the Senate. Just 150 substantive bills passed in the next session of Congress, the Pew Research Center found. Key pieces of legislation included the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement and several emergency Covid relief measures once the pandemic hit. But as was the case after the 2014 midterms, divided government led to several high-profile clashes, including a 35-day government shutdown and Trump’s first impeachment. Were Democrats punished for the lack of productivity? No. They won full control of Washington in 2020, with Joe Biden taking the White House. 2022: Biden’s first midterm saw Republicans regain control of the House while falling short in the Senate. But it was a similar story as the previous two midterms, with just 84 substantive bills passing during the next congressional session, according to Pew. That included a spending agreement following a debt ceiling fight that spooked the markets and led to a downgrade of the U.S. credit rating. Republicans also fought bitterly with each other, eventually deposing Speaker Kevin McCarthy mid-session. But did Republicans pay a political price? Not quite. The GOP again won a trifecta in the 2024 election, with Trump returning to the White House. 2026: And two years later, voters ushered in huge Democratic majorities after deciding, according to NBC News exit polling, that Trump failed to fulfill his promises to make life more affordable. Will Democrats deliver on that? And if they don’t, will they suffer politically for it in the 2028 presidential election? Based on the lessons of the last dozen years, the onus is on the president and his party to work with the new majorities in Congress, because voters have shown that they’ll punish the party in the White House for dysfunction and paralysis in Washington. 📺 Related: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said on “Meet the Press” that he’s open to working with Trump to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans. Read more → Democrats look to 2027 races for governor to build on gains in the South By Bridget Bowman, Alexandra Marquez and Adam Edelman Democrats calling on their party to invest in the South after historic victories this year won’t have to wait until 2028, with races for governor in Mississippi, Louisiana and Kentucky ahead in 2027. These contests will come just one year after Democrats flipped Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, governorships in Texas and Georgia and House districts across the South for the first time in decades. And Southern Democrats are confident their party has taken notice. “The South is competitive for Democrats,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chaired the Democratic Governors Association this year, told NBC News. “As a Southern Democrat, we were often overlooked, underfunded, sometimes even looked down upon. But we have scrapped our way back to the table.” Beshear, a possible presidential candidate, won a second term by 5 points two years ago and cannot run again due to term limits. In 2023, Democrat Brandon Presley lost in Mississippi to GOP Gov. Tate Reeves, who is term-limited, by 3 points. And former Democratic Gov. John Bel Edwards won two terms in Louisiana in 2015 and 2019 before Republican Gov. Jeff Landry won the office in 2023. This year, Democrat Scott Colom notched a historic Senate victory in Mississippi and Democrat Jamie Davis came close to winning Louisiana. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Legal fight over 20,000 California ballots ends as appeals court approves DOJ dismissal
articles.summary: A federal appeals court approved the Justice Department’s bid to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots until officials could verify the immigration statuses of recipients it alleged were noncitizens.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — A federal appeals court on Monday approved the Justice Department’s bid to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots until officials could verify the immigration statuses of recipients it alleged were noncitizens. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decision marked the official end to a flurry of litigation in California immediately preceding the competitive and high-stakes November midterms. Federal prosecutors who brought the lawsuit previously said that their efforts would become moot after Election Day, since local officials would no longer be able to prevent ballots from being counted. The contested ballots were at the heart of a protracted legal battle between the Trump administration and California over the eligibility of voters in the heavily Democratic state, and came amid broader federal scrutiny of local elections nationally. The Trump administration also issued a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler candidate controversy, but moved to drop those efforts two days after former Rep. Mary Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats’ 56th senator, as part of a Democratic midterm blowout. A related lawsuit filed against the Justice Department by the labor unions and pro-voting groups was also dismissed this month. The lawsuit came after the federal government threatened to charge California state election workers who counted the contested ballots and issued criminal grand jury subpoenas to clerks in Los Angeles and Orange counties. It argued that the Justice Department’s efforts risked interfering with the lawful administration of state and federal election law, since ballot processing was already underway when the federal government issued the subpoenas.

articles.title: What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
articles.summary: The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections .

As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.

All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.

Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.

How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.

The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.

The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran , aggressive immigration raids and corruption.

Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas , Mississippi and South Carolina.

Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.

Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.

What will Democrats do with their majority?

Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.

But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.

In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.

Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.

Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.

Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.

On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.

He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.

While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.

Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed , for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.

“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.

Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.

The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.

While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.

He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer , who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.

“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.

“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”

Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.

“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.

articles.title: Unsealed warrant documents for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid reveal decades-long scope of investigation
articles.summary: The redacted search warrant for Homeland Security Investigations' raid on Ilhan Omar's Washington D.C. home was released, with phone and passport seized.
articles.body: Heavily redacted versions of documents used to justify a search warrant and raid on the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., were released to the public Monday evening. Despite the level of redaction, the documents provide more insight into the scope of the investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman. In an ex parte brief in support of an affidavit for a search warrant, federal prosecutors say they're searching for all "records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of [redacted], those violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, and occurring between 1980 to the present (the 'Target Offenses)." While accounts vary, even from the congresswoman herself, Omar was born in 1981 or 1982. She does not have a birth certificate. She came to the United States in 1995 with her father. Fox News Digital confirmed just after the Oct. 12 raid of her home, that investigators were looking into alleged immigration fraud, potentially related to how Omar and her father filled out her immigration paperwork. In another document, arguing that the court mischaracterized the government's arguments in ex parte proceedings, prosecutors make it clear that the investigation into Omar spans decades. "The United States believes that ILHAN has committed [REDACTED] crimes over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress," the document says. Fox News Digital reached out to a spokesperson for Omar. In a rare move, Obama-appointed federal Judge James Boasberg ordered the documents' release last week, telling the Department of Justice (DOJ) to submit proposed redactions before the materials were made public on Monday. Judge Boasberg, in order dated October 9, 2026, agreed initially to seal the documents due to "such reasonable grounds to believe the disclosure will result in flight from prosecution, destruction of or tampering with evidence, intimidation of potential witnesses, and serious jeopardy to the investigation." Search warrants typically remain sealed until there is an arrest in a criminal case. Fifteen media outlets, led by The New York Times, along with watchdog group Judicial Watch, sued President Donald Trump's DOJ for the release of the documents used to conduct the raid of a sitting congresswoman's residence. The outlets claimed that viewing the documents was in the public interest, while the government attempted to block the release by arguing that it was a violation of investigative protocol. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE PAVES WAY TO UNSEAL ILHAN OMAR SEARCH WARRANT IN BLOW TO TRUMP'S DOJ Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided on Oct. 12, 2026 — an unprecedented action to take against a sitting lawmaker, especially when there is less than a month until the Election Day where they are seeking reelection. The raid did not impact Omar in winning a fifth term in the House of Representatives. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the chief investigative body of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), conducted the raid last month. Omar's personal phone, computer and passport were seized as evidence in the search. Authorities are also in possession of her DNA. Additionally, the lawmaker's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily submitted to questions from investigators during the week of the raid. Investigators are probing whether Omar or her late father — or both — lied on her citizenship paperwork, sources told Fox News Digital. In a motion seeking to prevent the federal search warrant for the raid from being unsealed, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the congresswoman's "real name." REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES That news caused speculation that Omar married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, to resurface. The pair married in 2009, and divorced in 2017. Omar has not been charged with a crime and has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. She has characterized the investigation as politically motivated, saying President Donald Trump is targeting her. "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," her office said in a statement after the raid. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." The Somali-born congresswoman came to the United States as a child in 1995, after decades of civil unrest in her home country. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, served as a colonel in the Somali National Army under the brutal Siad Barre regime. articles.title: Trump uses backdrop of DOJ to bash Gavin Newsom on death row commutations
articles.summary: President Donald Trump gave his speech at the Justice Department headquarters — a rarity for a president — and invited victims’ family members to speak onstage.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Monday delivered remarks at the Justice Department’s headquarters in Washington, denouncing Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan for commuting the death sentences of more than 500 convicted murderers. It is rare for a president to speak at the Justice Department. Trump last did so in March 2025, when he called for jailing his perceived political foes. This time, he took swipes at Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential contender, whom he called a “terrible” governor. “He stood with the murderers and the child slayers, but today we say the American people stand with you. We stand with you. We’re not going to let this happen,” Trump said, without elaborating on how his administration could intervene. The death row sentences being commuted by Newsom all stem from state cases. Trump also announced several new executive actions, including a presidential directive that he said ordered the DOJ to seek the death penalty for “child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims.” He added that the order would direct the attorney general to expedite the execution of federal death row inmates. The president brought relatives of several victims onstage, who at times became emotional when describing how their loved ones had died. Some who spoke were the parents of victims whose killings made national news for years and sparked changes to the law. Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was abducted from her home in Petaluma in 1993 before being killed, said he was “outraged” by Newsom’s actions. Actress Winona Ryder had offered a $200,000 reward for information at the time Polly went missing. The man convicted in her death, Richard Allen Davis, had a record and was previously released from prison — his conviction helped lead to California’s “three strikes” law that increased prison sentences for repeat offenders. Another speaker, Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was killed by Robert Boyd Rhodes, asked Newsom to “face” her as she described her son’s death. “His most feared thing was the dark. That night, Michael learned that the boogeyman was real. Mikey was raped, sodomized and tortured for 10 hours, from the very first inflicted stab wound to the last,” Friend said, choking up at one point while adding, “Sorry, this is so very hard.” “Governor Newsom erased that with the swipe of a pen, without notifying the families,” Friend said of Rhodes’ death sentence. Newsom responded to the DOJ event in a video message on social media, accusing the president of “selling” pardons and benefiting his associates. “To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That’s why every person, every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. No one walks out. Donald Trump’s criminals, they walk out,” Newsom said. “A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends — that’s not law enforcement. That’s a protection racket,” the governor added. He previously said, in announcing his plan, that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.” Trump wrapped up the somber event by shaking hands with the victims’ family members, some of whom had been in tears only minutes before. But the tone quickly shifted when his campaign anthem — the upbeat “YMCA” — played as he left the stage. Newsom and Trump’s back-and-forth comes amid a series of botched executions across the country. Last week prison staffers in Texas struggled to find a vein on Reinaldo Dennes, resulting in an execution that lasted over an hour as Dennes cried out in pain. And in September, Christa Pike, the sole woman on Tennessee’s death row, became the first person to survive a lethal injection. She was placed on a ventilator and regained consciousness days later. Support for the death penalty in the U.S. has generally been declining since a high of 80% in 1994, but Americans have complicated feelings about capital punishment. A Gallup poll this month found that 49% of U.S. adults favored the death penalty for those convicted of murder, with 45% opposed. But a Pew Research Center survey in August found that 66% of Americans were in favor of the death penalty for those convicted of murder, though 59% said the death penalty was not a crime deterrent. There is also a partisan gap, with Democrats increasingly opposing the death penalty.
